reigns.tagline: The man who sank a fleet with sticks in the mud
reigns.cameToPower: Won the Battle of Bạch Đằng
reigns.previously: A thousand years of rule from China. Now the Tang dynasty has fallen.
paragraphs: Since 111 BC the Red River delta had been ruled from China. There were risings, most famously the Trưng sisters' in AD 40, but none of them lasted. Then the Tang dynasty fell apart and local strongmen took charge. One of them, Dương Đình Nghệ, was murdered in 937 by his own officer, Kiều Công Tiễn. Nghệ's son-in-law, a tough commander named Ngô Quyền, came looking for revenge.

Tiễn begged the Southern Han, a new kingdom in south China, to send help. Ngô Quyền killed him before it came, then waited for the Han fleet at the mouth of the Bạch Đằng River. His men drove iron-tipped stakes into the riverbed. At high tide he lured the ships upstream, then hit back as the water fell. The fleet was ripped open on the stakes, and the Han prince Liu Hongcao died with it.

In 939 Ngô Quyền declared himself king and set up his court at Cổ Loa, an ancient citadel near today's Hanoi. He had only five years. He died in 944, aged about 46, and his brother-in-law Dương Tam Kha pushed the young sons aside and seized the throne.

claims.text: Ngô Quyền's men planted iron-tipped stakes in the Bạch Đằng riverbed to wreck the Han fleet.
claims.note: Told in the Vietnamese annals. The stakes dug out of the river so far are dated to the 1288 battle, which copied the trick.

claims.text: The Southern Han prince Liu Hongcao was killed in the battle.
claims.note: Chinese histories of the Southern Han record his death as well as the Vietnamese annals.

reigns.hook: Ngô Quyền's sons are still boys. He has left the eldest in the care of their uncle, Dương Tam Kha, and Tam Kha is about to decide he would make a better king.

reigns.tagline: The guardian who kept the throne for himself
reigns.cameToPower: Seized the throne from the heir
reigns.previously: Ngô Quyền dies. His wife's brother is guarding the heir.
paragraphs: Ngô Quyền's queen was a daughter of Dương Đình Nghệ, the governor whose murder had started it all. Her brother, Dương Tam Kha, was the man Ngô Quyền trusted to look after his eldest son, Ngô Xương Ngập, when he died in 944. Tam Kha looked after himself instead. He took the throne and called himself Dương Bình Vương.

Xương Ngập ran for it and hid in the countryside, sheltered by a local chief while Tam Kha's men hunted him. The younger brother, Ngô Xương Văn, stayed at court. Tam Kha adopted him as his own son, which kept a Ngô boy close and under his eye.

In 950 trouble broke out in the villages west of the capital, and Tam Kha sent Xương Văn with two generals to crush it. On the march the young man talked the generals round. They turned the army back, surprised Tam Kha and took the throne for the Ngô. Xương Văn spared his uncle's life and gave him an estate to live on.

claims.text: Ngô Quyền left his son in Dương Tam Kha's care when he died.
claims.note: The Toàn thư says so, and it explains how Tam Kha was in a position to grab the throne.

claims.text: Ngô Xương Ngập survived by hiding in caves and haystacks while soldiers searched for him.
claims.note: The annals tell a dramatic escape story. The details read like later storytelling.

claims.text: Xương Văn spared Tam Kha because he was his mother's brother.
claims.note: The annals say the new king refused to kill his uncle and gave him an estate instead.

reigns.hook: Ngô Quyền's sons have their father's throne back. The trouble is that two brothers now want to wear the crown, and the strongmen in the countryside have stopped listening to either.

reigns.title: The Later Ngô Kings
reigns.tagline: Two brothers share a crown and lose the country
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Ngô Quyền's sons; Tam Kha's nephews
reigns.cameToPower: Turned the army on Dương Tam Kha
reigns.reignEnded: Xương Văn killed by an arrow
reigns.previously: Xương Văn turns his army round and topples Dương Tam Kha.
paragraphs: Ngô Xương Văn could have kept the throne for himself. Instead, in 951, he fetched his elder brother Xương Ngập out of hiding and the two ruled together, the Later Ngô kings. Xương Văn took the title Nam Tấn Vương and Xương Ngập Thiên Sách Vương. The annals say the elder brother soon pushed the younger aside, but he died in 954 and Xương Văn ruled alone.

Their real problem was outside the palace. Local strongmen with their own walls and soldiers had stopped obeying Cổ Loa. The brothers marched against one of them, Đinh Bộ Lĩnh at Hoa Lư, and got nowhere. The famous story is that they held his son Đinh Liễn hostage and threatened to kill him, and Bộ Lĩnh told them to go ahead.

In 965 Xương Văn went to put down two rebel villages. He was shot by an archer hidden in an ambush and died. Ngô Xương Xí, Xương Ngập's son, held on to a small patch of land, but the kingdom was gone. The country split between twelve warlords.

claims.text: When the Ngô kings threatened to kill Đinh Liễn, his father ordered his own archers to shoot at the boy.
claims.note: A story in the Toàn thư meant to show Đinh Bộ Lĩnh's iron will. It cannot be checked, and the boy lived.

claims.text: Xương Văn was killed by an arrow from an ambush while attacking rebel villages in 965.
claims.note: The annals give this account. The death in 965 is accepted; the details come only from the much later chronicle.

claims.text: Xương Ngập sidelined his younger brother once he was brought back.
claims.note: The Toàn thư says so. With so little evidence, it may be a moral tale about ingratitude.

reigns.hook: Twelve warlords now carve up the delta. One of them, a former buffalo boy from Hoa Lư called Đinh Bộ Lĩnh, means to beat every one of the others.

reigns.tagline: The buffalo boy who beat twelve warlords
reigns.previously: Ngô Quyền's line falls apart. Twelve warlords split the country.
paragraphs: Legend says Đinh Bộ Lĩnh grew up herding buffalo near Hoa Lư and led the village boys in mock battles, with reeds for flags. Grown up, he did it for real. After Ngô Quyền's line lost its grip, twelve warlords had carved up the delta. Đinh Bộ Lĩnh beat them one by one, and people called him Vạn Thắng Vương, the king of ten thousand victories.

In 968 he went one better than Ngô Quyền and called himself emperor (hoàng đế). He named the country Đại Cồ Việt and made his capital at Hoa Lư, a fortress ringed by limestone crags. To keep China quiet he sent tribute to the new Song dynasty: emperor at home, king on paper abroad. He is remembered as Đinh Tiên Hoàng. Order came hard. The annals say he kept a cauldron of boiling oil and caged tigers at court for wrongdoers.

In 979 an official named Đỗ Thích murdered both the emperor and his eldest son, Đinh Liễn. The throne went to a little boy, Đinh Toàn, only five or six years old. The real power went to the commander of the army, Lê Hoàn.

claims.text: As a boy he led the village children in mock battles, using reeds as flags.
claims.note: A favourite story in the annals and local tradition, the kind told about founders after the fact.

claims.text: He kept a cauldron of boiling oil and tigers in a cage to punish criminals.
claims.note: Recorded in the Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư, written centuries later. Nobody knows if they were used or just a threat.

claims.text: Đỗ Thích killed the emperor after dreaming that a star fell into his mouth.
claims.note: The annals give this dream as his motive. It explains a murder neatly, which is reason enough to doubt it.

reigns.hook: The emperor and his heir are dead. The throne goes to a little boy, Đinh Toàn, and the power to the army chief, Lê Hoàn. In China, the Song smell a chance.

reigns.tagline: The boy emperor whose army chose someone else
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Small son of Đinh Bộ Lĩnh
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne after the murders
reigns.previously: Đinh Bộ Lĩnh and his eldest son are murdered in the palace.
paragraphs: With the emperor and his heir both murdered, the court at Hoa Lư crowned the only son left, Đinh Toàn, a little boy. His mother was the dowager empress Dương Vân Nga. Power went to the army commander, Lê Hoàn, as regent. The killer, the official Đỗ Thích, was caught and put to death.

Not everyone trusted the regent. Two of the old emperor's closest comrades, Đinh Điền and Nguyễn Bặc, thought Lê Hoàn was too close to the dowager and too keen on the throne. They raised troops. Lê Hoàn beat them and had them killed. A Ngô prince, Ngô Nhật Khánh, came by sea with a fleet from Champa, but a storm wrecked it before it reached Hoa Lư.

Then the Song got ready to invade. The generals would not go to war behind a child. In 980 the army hailed Lê Hoàn as emperor, and Đinh Toàn was set aside with a lesser title. History calls him Đinh Phế Đế, the deposed emperor. He lived on under the new ruler, and in 1001 he was killed by an arrow while campaigning beside Lê Hoàn.

claims.text: A storm wrecked Ngô Nhật Khánh's Cham fleet on its way to attack Hoa Lư in 979.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư. The storm is the kind of detail chronicles enjoy, but historians accept the failed attack.

claims.text: The generals said a child could not reward their efforts, and crowned Lê Hoàn instead.
claims.note: The annals give the army commander Phạm Cự Lượng a speech saying so. The words are the chronicler's; the army's backing is real.

claims.text: Đinh Toàn died in 1001, hit by an arrow on a campaign with Lê Hoàn.
claims.note: The Toàn thư records it. Some have wondered whether it was really an accident, but no source says otherwise.

reigns.hook: The army has its new emperor, and the boy's mother has handed him the dragon robe. Now Lê Hoàn has to face the Song army marching south.

reigns.tagline: The regent who took the robe and beat the Song
reigns.previously: Boy emperor Đinh Toàn faces a Song invasion with a regent in charge.
paragraphs: With a child on the throne at Hoa Lư, the Song got ready to invade in 980. The generals didn't want a boy leading them to war, so the army acclaimed the regent, Lê Hoàn, as emperor. The annals stage a grand scene: the boy's mother, the dowager empress Dương Vân Nga, laid the dragon robe on Lê Hoàn's shoulders herself. She later became his empress.

Lê Hoàn, remembered as Lê Đại Hành, met the Song in 981 and smashed them. Their general Hou Renbao was killed. The next year he turned south and sacked the capital of Champa. Then he patched things up with the Song, who accepted him as a tributary king. At home, the annals say, he held the first royal ploughing ceremony, steering a plough himself to bless the year's crops.
He reigned for a quarter of a century and had a lot of sons. He handed them provinces and troops to command, and never made the succession stick. When he died in 1005, they went for each other.

claims.text: Dương Vân Nga handed Lê Hoàn the dragon robe in front of the army.
claims.note: A dramatic scene in the annals, written long afterwards. Her later marriage to him is better attested.

claims.text: The Song general Hou Renbao was killed in the 981 war.
claims.note: Reported in both the Vietnamese annals and the official Song history.

claims.text: Lê Hoàn held the first royal ploughing ceremony in Vietnam.
claims.note: Only the later annals record it, and they liked giving old customs a famous founder.

reigns.hook: Lê Hoàn's sons are drawing their swords. The chosen heir will get the throne in the end, and keep it for three days.

reigns.tagline: The king who held court lying down
reigns.cameToPower: His men killed the new king
reigns.previously: Lê Hoàn dies. His sons fight over the throne for months.
paragraphs: Lê Hoàn's death set off months of fighting between his sons. The heir, Lê Long Việt, finally took the throne and lasted three days. Then men sent by his younger brother Long Đĩnh broke into the palace and killed him. Long Đĩnh, about nineteen, made himself emperor.

He is remembered as Lê Ngọa Triều, the king who held court lying down, supposedly because illness kept him from sitting up. The annals paint him as a monster. Their best-known story has him shave a monk's head and peel sugar cane on it, letting the knife slip so the man bled. But those annals were written for the dynasty that replaced him, which had every reason to blacken his name.

He died in late 1009, aged 23, leaving a son far too small to rule. The court had no appetite for another child emperor. Its eyes turned to the commander of the palace guard, a man raised by Buddhist monks: Lý Công Uẩn.

claims.text: He held audiences lying down because he was too ill to sit.
claims.note: The annals give illness as the reason. The nickname is real; the explanation comes from his enemies' historians.

claims.text: He peeled sugar cane on a monk's shaven head for fun.
claims.note: Told by later court historians working for the Lý, who needed the last Early Lê king to look unfit to rule.

claims.text: His brother Lê Long Việt reigned for only three days.
claims.note: All the annals agree on the short reign and the murder.

reigns.hook: The court offers the crown to Lý Công Uẩn. Within a year he will leave the fortress of Hoa Lư behind and build a new capital on the Red River.

reigns.tagline: The temple boy who founded Hanoi
reigns.previously: Lê Long Đĩnh dies at 23. His son is a baby; the court looks elsewhere.
paragraphs: Lý Công Uẩn grew up in a Buddhist pagoda, raised by monks. One of them, the monk Vạn Hạnh, is said to have spotted his talent and pushed his rise. He joined the palace guard and climbed to its command. When Lê Long Đĩnh died, the court made him emperor. He is remembered as Lý Thái Tổ, founder of the Lý, the first Vietnamese dynasty to last more than a couple of generations.

In 1010 he issued the Edict on Moving the Capital (Chiếu dời đô). Hoa Lư was a fortress, good for hiding, bad for ruling. He moved to Đại La, on the open plain by the Red River. As he arrived, the story goes, a golden dragon rose over the site, so he called it Thăng Long, the ascending dragon. It is the city we now call Hanoi.

He poured money into Buddhist temples and had many new monks ordained. He ruled for over eighteen years and died in the spring of 1028. Before he was even buried, three of his sons brought troops to the palace to take the throne from the heir.

claims.text: He named Thăng Long after seeing a golden dragon rise over the site.
claims.note: The story is in the annals. The name was clearly chosen for its good omen, whatever anyone saw.

claims.text: The monk Vạn Hạnh backed his rise to the throne.
claims.note: The annals give Vạn Hạnh prophecies about the Lý. How much he really steered events is unclear.

claims.text: He issued an edict in 1010 moving the capital from Hoa Lư.
claims.note: The text of the Chiếu dời đô survives in the Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư.

reigns.hook: Three princes and their men are at the palace gates. The heir, Lý Phật Mã, has one thing going for him: a general called Lê Phụng Hiểu.

reigns.tagline: He beat his brothers, then dreamed up a pagoda
reigns.previously: Lý Thái Tổ dies. Three of his sons rise against the heir.
paragraphs: Lý Phật Mã's first test came before his father was buried. Three of his brothers marched on the palace to seize it. His general Lê Phụng Hiểu led the guard out and cut one of the princes down, and the revolt fell apart. It went down as the rebellion of the three princes. Phật Mã, remembered as Lý Thái Tông, pardoned the two who survived.

He spent much of his reign at war. In the northern mountains he fought the Nùng chief Nùng Trí Cao, who rose more than once. In 1044 he led an army deep into Champa, and the Cham king was killed in the fighting.

In 1049 he built the One Pillar Pagoda, a small shrine set on a single pillar in a pond, like a lotus on its stem. The story is that he had dreamed of the bodhisattva Quan Âm seated on a lotus, reaching down to him. He died in 1054 after 26 years, with a grown son ready to take over.

claims.text: He built the One Pillar Pagoda after dreaming of Quan Âm on a lotus.
claims.note: The dream comes from the annals. The pagoda you can visit in Hanoi was rebuilt in 1955 after French troops blew it up in 1954.

claims.text: His general Lê Phụng Hiểu crushed the revolt of three princes in 1028.
claims.note: Recorded in detail in the Vietnamese annals.

claims.text: The king of Champa was killed during the 1044 campaign.
claims.note: The annals record his death; Cham records also show a change of king around this time.

reigns.hook: His son inherits a confident kingdom and wants it to sound like one. First comes a new name. Then Champa, the southern neighbour, gets another visit.

reigns.tagline: He named Đại Việt and built a temple to Confucius
reigns.previously: Lý Thái Tông dies after 26 years. His grown son takes over.
paragraphs: Lý Thánh Tông started by renaming the country Đại Việt, Great Viet. The name stuck, give or take a few breaks, for the next 750 years. In 1070 he built the Temple of Literature (Văn Miếu) in Thăng Long, dedicated to Confucius. It still stands in Hanoi, a walled garden of courtyards and shrines in the middle of the traffic.

In 1069 he invaded Champa and captured its king, Rudravarman III, called Chế Củ in Vietnamese. To buy his freedom, the king gave up three districts on Champa's northern edge. It was an early step in Đại Việt's long push south.

While Thánh Tông was away at war, his consort Ỷ Lan ran the government, and ran it well. Legend says he first saw her as a village girl leaning against a tree, ignoring the royal procession everyone else had rushed out to watch. She gave him the son he had waited years for. When Thánh Tông died in 1072, that boy was not yet six.

claims.text: He met Ỷ Lan when she was a village girl leaning against a tree.
claims.note: A romantic story built around her name, which means 'leaning on the orchid tree'. The annals confirm only that she was a royal consort.

claims.text: The captured Cham king gave up three districts for his release.
claims.note: Recorded in the Vietnamese annals and accepted by modern historians of Champa.

claims.text: Ỷ Lan governed while the king was on campaign in 1069.
claims.note: The annals credit her with keeping the country calm while he was away.

reigns.hook: A five-year-old is king. His mother wants power, the old general Lý Thường Kiệt wants a fight, and Song China is getting ready to give him one.

reigns.tagline: 56 years, a war with China and a ghostly poem
reigns.cameToPower: Succeeded his father as a child
reigns.previously: Lý Thánh Tông dies. His son is not yet six years old.
paragraphs: Lý Nhân Tông came to the throne a small boy, so others ran things: his mother Ỷ Lan and the veteran general Lý Thường Kiệt. Ỷ Lan wanted no rivals. The annals say she had the widowed senior empress, Thượng Dương, put to death along with her maids. Meanwhile the court built a state run by scholars. Đại Việt held its first civil service exam in 1075 and opened the Imperial Academy (Quốc Tử Giám) in 1076.

The Song were planning an invasion. Lý Thường Kiệt didn't wait for it. In 1075–76 he struck first, crossing into China and sacking Yongzhou. When the Song army came south in 1077, he held it at the Như Nguyệt River. One night, the story goes, a voice from a riverside temple recited a poem: the mountains and rivers of the south belong to the southern emperor, as written in the book of heaven.

That poem, 'Nam quốc sơn hà', is often called Vietnam's first declaration of independence. The Song gave up and went home. Nhân Tông went on to reign for 56 years, longer than any other Vietnamese monarch. He had no son, so the throne went to a nephew.

claims.text: Ỷ Lan had the senior empress Thượng Dương and her maids killed.
claims.note: A story in the annals. It fits the politics but no other source confirms it.

claims.text: The poem 'Nam quốc sơn hà' was recited at night from a temple to rally the troops.
claims.note: Later sources tell the tale. Who wrote the poem, and whether it was first used in this war, is debated.

claims.text: Lý Nhân Tông reigned longer than any other Vietnamese monarch.
claims.note: His 56 years, from 1072 to 1128, are a record in every king list.

reigns.hook: A nephew, Lý Thần Tông, inherits a strong kingdom. Over the next century the Lý will slowly lose it to regents, favourites, famine and a clan of fishermen from the coast.

reigns.tagline: The nephew said to be a reborn monk
reigns.cameToPower: Adopted heir of his childless uncle
reigns.previously: Lý Nhân Tông dies after 56 years. A nephew takes his place.
paragraphs: Lý Nhân Tông had no son, so he raised his brother's boy, Lý Dương Hoán, as his heir. A strange story came with him. His father had prayed for a son to the monk Từ Đạo Hạnh, a famous wonder-worker of the Thầy pagoda. The monk promised to be reborn in the family, then died, and soon afterwards Dương Hoán was born.

He became king as Lý Thần Tông at about eleven. The kingdom was still strong. In 1128, and again in 1132, armies from the Khmer empire of Angkor raided the southern province of Nghệ An, the second time with Cham help. Both times they were driven off. The court also let soldiers go home in turns to farm their fields, so the army fed itself.

Thần Tông died in 1138, only about 22. Legend says a mysterious illness was turning him into a tiger until a monk cured him, and that he died soon after anyway. His heir, Thiên Tộ, was two years old. Child kings would be the Lý story from now on.

claims.text: Lý Thần Tông was the reincarnation of the monk Từ Đạo Hạnh.
claims.note: A Buddhist story in the annals and in the Thầy pagoda's own tradition. It shows how close the Lý throne was to the monasteries.

claims.text: Khmer armies from Angkor attacked Nghệ An in 1128 and 1132 and were beaten off.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư. They match the aggressive reign of Suryavarman II, builder of Angkor Wat.

claims.text: In his last illness the king grew fur and claws, and a monk cured him.
claims.note: Folk tradition around the monk Nguyễn Minh Không. Nobody takes the tiger literally.

reigns.hook: A two-year-old is king now. Behind the throne stand his mother and her favourite, a smooth court official called Đỗ Anh Vũ.

reigns.tagline: The toddler king and his mother's favourite
reigns.cameToPower: Inherited the throne as a toddler
reigns.previously: Lý Thần Tông dies young. His heir is two years old.
paragraphs: Lý Anh Tông, born Lý Thiên Tộ, was crowned at about two, so for years the court belonged to the grown-ups. The strongest of them was the official Đỗ Anh Vũ, who ran the palace and, the annals say, shared the queen mother's bed. In 1150 a group of officials had him arrested. The queen mother got him off, and he took his revenge on the men who had tried to bring him down.

Đỗ Anh Vũ died in 1158, and the king turned to a very different man, the honest general Tô Hiến Thành. The reign had its successes. In 1149 the court opened a harbour at Vân Đồn in the islands of the northeast, where foreign ships came to trade. A man claiming to be a son of Nhân Tông led a rising in 1140, and it was put down.

Anh Tông reigned 37 years. Near the end he removed his eldest son as heir after a scandal with palace women, and picked a younger boy, Long Trát, only about a year old. He died in 1175 and left Tô Hiến Thành as the child's guardian.

claims.text: Đỗ Anh Vũ was the queen mother's lover.
claims.note: The Toàn thư says so. Court chroniclers often explained a favourite's power this way, so it may be gossip.

claims.text: Vân Đồn was opened as a port for foreign merchants in 1149.
claims.note: Recorded in the annals, and archaeologists have found traces of the old harbour.

claims.text: The eldest prince was disinherited for an affair with palace women.
claims.note: The annals give this reason. It may cover a power struggle over the succession.

reigns.hook: A two-year-old king, a dowager who wants her favourite son back, and one honest man standing between them. Tô Hiến Thành will not be bought.

reigns.tagline: Palaces and pleasure while the country starved
reigns.previously: Lý Anh Tông dies. Tô Hiến Thành guards a toddler king.
paragraphs: Lý Cao Tông, born Long Trát, was a baby when he was crowned. His regent, Tô Hiến Thành, is remembered as the model of an honest minister. The queen mother wanted her disinherited son back on the throne and, the story goes, tried to bribe Tô Hiến Thành's wife with gold. He refused to change his mind. He died in 1179, and the good years died with him.

Cao Tông grew up loving hunting, building and parties. The chronicles say he spent while famine, bandits and revolts spread. In 1208 a local strongman, Phạm Du, rebelled. The king executed the general sent to stop him, on Phạm Du's word, and the general's officer Quách Bốc stormed Thăng Long in revenge. The king fled to the hills.

The crown prince, Lý Sảm, fled to the coast, to the Trần, a rich family of fishermen and traders with their own fighters. He married their daughter, Trần Thị Dung, and the Trần army took Thăng Long back. Cao Tông came home in 1209, rescued by men who now expected a share of the power. He died the next year.

claims.text: Tô Hiến Thành turned down a bribe of gold sent to his wife by the queen mother.
claims.note: A favourite story in the annals of the incorruptible minister. It may be polished, but his reputation is solid.

claims.text: Cao Tông wasted money on palaces and pleasure while his people starved.
claims.note: So say the chronicles, which were written under the Trần. Blaming the last kings helped explain why the Lý fell.

claims.text: Rebels drove the king out of Thăng Long in 1209.
claims.note: All the annals record Quách Bốc's capture of the capital and the king's flight.

reigns.hook: Cao Tông is dead. His son is king, his wife is a Trần, and her family's soldiers guard the palace. The new king cannot do much without them.

reigns.tagline: The king who gave the crown to a little girl
reigns.previously: Lý Cao Tông dies. The Trần clan has a grip on his son.
paragraphs: Lý Huệ Tông came to the throne at about 16, and from the start he was trapped between his mother and his wife. His mother hated the Trần and, the annals say, tried to poison Trần Thị Dung. More than once the young king fled the capital with his wife to the camp of her brother, Trần Tự Khánh, who led the Trần army. The country was full of rival warlords, and some of them set up other Lý princes as kings.

The Trần won those fights, and each win tied the king tighter to them. Huệ Tông fell ill, and people said he was going mad. Thị Dung's cousin Trần Thủ Độ took command of the palace guard. By the 1220s nothing happened at court without him.

Huệ Tông had no son. In 1224 he passed the throne to his little daughter, Phật Kim, and went off to a pagoda as a monk. Two years later, the famous story goes, Trần Thủ Độ found him pulling weeds and told him to pull them up by the roots. The ex-king understood, and hanged himself.

claims.text: Huệ Tông's mother tried to poison his Trần wife.
claims.note: The Toàn thư says so. The chronicle was written under the Trần, who had every reason to blacken the Lý side.

claims.text: Lý Huệ Tông went mad.
claims.note: The annals describe fits and odd behaviour. They also gave the Trần a reason for taking over.

claims.text: Trần Thủ Độ hinted to him, with a remark about pulling weeds by the roots, that he should die.
claims.note: A famous anecdote in the annals. That Trần Thủ Độ forced his death is widely accepted; the weed line sounds like storytelling.

reigns.hook: A six-year-old girl is now empress, the only one Vietnam will ever have. Trần Thủ Độ has plans for her, and they start with a husband.

reigns.tagline: Vietnam's only empress, and she was six
reigns.reignEnded: Handed the throne to her husband
reigns.previously: Lý Huệ Tông gives up the throne and becomes a monk.
paragraphs: Lý Chiêu Hoàng, born Lý Phật Kim, is the only woman ever to reign over Vietnam in her own right, and she was about six when she did it. She ruled nothing. Trần Thủ Độ packed the palace with his relatives and married the little empress to his young kinsman Trần Cảnh, a boy of seven.

In the last lunar month of 1225, which fell in January 1226, she handed the throne to her husband. After more than two centuries the Lý dynasty was over. Trần Thủ Độ made sure it stayed that way. He is said to have forced her father, the ex-emperor Huệ Tông, now a monk, to kill himself in 1226, and to have massacred Lý clansmen.

Her own life had more twists to come. In 1237, because she had no surviving son, Trần Cảnh was made to take her elder sister, Princess Thuận Thiên, instead. She was his brother Trần Liễu's wife, and already pregnant. Later she married a general, Lê Phụ Trần, and lived until 1278.

claims.text: Trần Thủ Độ forced the ex-emperor Huệ Tông to kill himself.
claims.note: The annals say so outright. They were written under the Trần, but historians generally accept it.

claims.text: Trần Thủ Độ massacred members of the Lý clan.
claims.note: The annals tell of Lý kin buried alive in a pit during a ceremony. The scale and details may be exaggerated.

claims.text: Trần Cảnh was made to take his pregnant sister-in-law as empress in 1237.
claims.note: Recorded in the annals, along with the revolt it set off from his brother Trần Liễu.

reigns.hook: The Trần hold the throne through a boy emperor. Trần Thủ Độ is the real ruler, and far to the north the Mongols are swallowing one kingdom after another.

reigns.tagline: A boy king, a ruthless kinsman and the first Mongol storm
reigns.cameToPower: His child bride handed him the throne
reigns.previously: The child empress Lý Chiêu Hoàng hands the throne to her boy husband.
paragraphs: Trần Cảnh was seven when his child bride gave him the crown. The real ruler was his kinsman Trần Thủ Độ, a hard man who stamped out what was left of the Lý and kept the court in his fist for decades. In 1237, because the empress had no son, Thủ Độ made Cảnh take a new wife: Princess Thuận Thiên, the wife of his elder brother Trần Liễu, already pregnant. Liễu rose in revolt. The young emperor fled to a monastery on Yên Tử mountain and had to be talked into coming home.

Then came the Mongols. In January 1258 an army under Uriyangkhadai rode down from Yunnan, routed the Vietnamese and took Thăng Long, which the court had abandoned. The emperor asked Thủ Độ whether to give in. His reply became famous: my head has not yet fallen to the ground, so Your Majesty need not worry. Within weeks the invaders, worn down by the heat and hit by a counter-attack, pulled back north. The Mongol deck tells it from their side.

Soon after, Thái Tông did something new. He handed the throne to his grown-up son and stayed on as retired emperor (thái thượng hoàng), guiding from behind. The Trần would do this again and again, so each heir learned the job while the old king was still alive to help.

claims.text: Trần Thủ Độ told the emperor that his head had not yet fallen, so there was nothing to worry about.
claims.note: The line comes from the Toàn thư, compiled two centuries later. It fits his character, but the exact words can't be checked.

claims.text: In 1237 the emperor was made to marry his elder brother's pregnant wife.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư and accepted by modern historians such as Keith Taylor.

claims.text: The young emperor ran away to Yên Tử and Thủ Độ fetched him back.
claims.note: Told in the Toàn thư. The flight is likely; the polished dialogue around it looks like the chroniclers' work.

reigns.hook: The Mongols have gone, for now. A new emperor must rebuild a burned capital while the Mongol empire, soon to be ruled by Kublai Khan, keeps its eye on the south.

reigns.tagline: Paid Kublai his tribute, but never knelt
reigns.previously: The Mongols sack Thăng Long and leave. Thái Tông steps aside.
paragraphs: Thánh Tông took over a burned capital and set about rebuilding it, with his father close by as retired emperor. To the north, Kublai Khan now ruled the Mongols and in 1271 named his dynasty the Yuan. He wanted proof of obedience. Thánh Tông sent tribute and polite letters. When Yuan envoys demanded that he come to court in person, he always found a reason not to.

At home the Trần kept power in the family. Princes married princesses, cousins married cousins, and the top army posts went to royal relatives. It was clannish, but it made a ruling family that fought as one. In 1272 the scholar Lê Văn Hưu finished the Đại Việt sử ký, the country's first official history. In 1278 Thánh Tông handed the throne to his son and, as retired emperor, stayed on to guide him.

claims.text: The Trần married inside the clan on purpose, to keep the throne in the family.
claims.note: Plain from the marriages in the Toàn thư; historians such as Keith Taylor treat it as deliberate policy.

claims.text: Lê Văn Hưu finished the first official history of Đại Việt in 1272.
claims.note: The book itself is lost, but the Toàn thư records it and quotes his comments.

claims.text: Thánh Tông refused Yuan demands that he come to court in person.
claims.note: Both the Vietnamese annals and the Yuan records describe the demands and the excuses.

reigns.hook: Kublai Khan is running out of patience. A young new emperor, Trần Nhân Tông, is about to face the full weight of the Yuan empire.

reigns.tagline: Beat Kublai's armies twice, then went off to be a monk
reigns.previously: Trần Thánh Tông steps aside for his son as the Yuan lose patience.
paragraphs: Kublai wanted a road through Đại Việt to attack Champa. Nhân Tông said no. In early 1285 the Yuan came anyway: a huge army under Kublai's son Toghan from the north, and Sogetu from Champa in the south. The old retired emperor called village elders to the Diên Hồng palace and asked: peace or war? Fight, they shouted. Soldiers tattooed Sát Thát, kill the Tatars, on their arms.

The court gave up Thăng Long, fell back, then struck hard. Sogetu was killed and Toghan retreated. In 1287 the Yuan returned. The commander-in-chief, as in 1285, was the Prince of Hưng Đạo, Trần Quốc Tuấn, whose fiery Proclamation to the Officers had rallied the army. He copied Ngô Quyền. In April 1288 stakes were planted in the Bạch Đằng River, the Yuan fleet was caught as the tide fell, and its admiral Omar was taken.

Toghan got away north. Nhân Tông then sent tribute to Kublai anyway: winning was enough, and peace was cheaper. In 1293 he gave up the throne, and later went to live as a monk on Yên Tử mountain, where he founded the Trúc Lâm (Bamboo Forest) school of Zen. The Mongol deck tells these wars from Kublai's side.

claims.text: At the Diên Hồng conference the village elders all shouted for war.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư, written long after. The meeting probably happened; the single roar reads like a set piece.

claims.text: Soldiers tattooed Sát Thát, kill the Tatars, on their arms.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư. Tattooing was common among Trần soldiers, so historians generally accept it.

claims.text: Retreating in 1285, Toghan escaped hidden inside a bronze tube.
claims.note: A Vietnamese tradition recorded in the annals. It cannot be checked, and it makes a suspiciously perfect humiliation for the invader.

reigns.hook: The Mongols are beaten and Nhân Tông's son, Trần Anh Tông, is king. The Trần's best days are behind them; weak kings, a fake prince and a Cham warrior king lie ahead.

reigns.tagline: He traded his sister for two provinces
reigns.previously: Trần Nhân Tông gives up the throne and heads for the mountains.
paragraphs: Trần Anh Tông took over a country that had just beaten the Mongols twice. He started badly. The story goes that his father came down from retirement and found him asleep, drunk, in the middle of the day. The young king was so ashamed he wrote out an apology and gave up drinking.

His big deal was in the south. In 1306 he married his sister, Princess Huyền Trân, to the Cham king Jaya Simhavarman III (Chế Mân), and Champa handed over two districts in return. The Cham king died the next year. Cham custom expected his queen to die on his funeral pyre, so Anh Tông sent the official Trần Khắc Chung to get her out, and she was brought home by sea.

Relations with Champa soured after that. In 1312 Anh Tông marched south and took the Cham king Chế Chí prisoner. In 1314 he followed the Trần custom and stepped down for his son, then ruled on as retired emperor until he died in 1320.

claims.text: Princess Huyền Trân was married to the Cham king in exchange for two districts.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư. The land became the Vietnamese prefectures of Thuận and Hóa, around today's Huế.

claims.text: Trần Khắc Chung had an affair with the princess on the long voyage home.
claims.note: The Toàn thư hints at it, and later writers made a romance of it. There is no real evidence.

claims.text: Anh Tông gave up drinking after his father caught him drunk.
claims.note: An improving story from the annals about a well-behaved king. It may be true, but it is very tidy.

reigns.hook: Anh Tông's son is now king, and his father is still watching. The new king will hold real power for more than forty years, and use it on his own family.

reigns.previously: Trần Anh Tông steps down and hands his son the throne.
paragraphs: Trần Minh Tông was a boy of about 13 when his father stepped down for him in 1314. The old man kept an eye on things until he died in 1320. In 1318 Trần armies went south again and the Cham king fled. The court was still strong and still run by the Trần princes, who married each other to keep power in the family.

The ugly chapter came in 1328. Minh Tông's father-in-law and uncle, Trần Quốc Chẩn, stood in the way of naming the king's son by another wife as heir. Courtiers produced a servant who said Quốc Chẩn was plotting. The king locked him up in a pagoda and gave him no water, and he died. The charge was false, and years later the truth came out.
In 1329 Minh Tông handed the throne to that son, a boy of about ten, and became retired emperor. He went on running the court for almost thirty years, until his death in 1357.

claims.text: Trần Quốc Chẩn was starved to death in prison on a false charge.
claims.note: The Toàn thư tells it and says the accuser later confessed. The chronicle is our only source.

claims.text: Trần Khắc Chung advised the king that catching a tiger is easy but letting it go is hard.
claims.note: A famous line given to him by the annals, meaning the king should not release Quốc Chẩn. It may be the chronicler's.

claims.text: Minh Tông held power as retired emperor until 1357.
claims.note: All sources agree that the reigning kings of these years deferred to him.

reigns.hook: A ten-year-old boy is king, but his father has only moved next door. As long as Minh Tông lives, the throne belongs to him.

reigns.tagline: King in name while his father kept the power
reigns.previously: Trần Minh Tông retires but keeps his hands on the reins.
paragraphs: Trần Hiến Tông, born Trần Vượng, was about ten when he became king, and for his whole reign his father made the decisions. The palace school was in good hands. The great teacher Chu Văn An was in charge of the Imperial Academy and is said to have taught the young king.

The trouble came from the western mountains. Raiders from Ai Lao, the lands of the Lao, crossed into the frontier provinces. In 1334 the retired Minh Tông led an army west himself and drove them back. In 1335 another expedition went wrong, and the veteran official Đoàn Nhữ Hài drowned in a river while fighting there.
Hiến Tông died in 1341, aged about 22, with no son. Once again Minh Tông chose the next king, another of his sons, Trần Hạo, a boy of about five.

claims.text: Chu Văn An taught the young Hiến Tông.
claims.note: Vietnamese tradition says Minh Tông made him tutor to the crown prince. The annals' record of it is thin.

claims.text: Đoàn Nhữ Hài drowned during the 1335 campaign against Ai Lao.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư, which says the army was caught in an ambush.

claims.text: Real power stayed with the retired Minh Tông throughout the reign.
claims.note: The annals date the big decisions of these years to Minh Tông, not the young king.

reigns.hook: A five-year-old is king. While his father, the retired Minh Tông, lives the court stays in line, but when he dies the drinking, the debts and the corruption will start.

reigns.tagline: A boy king, a drunken court and seven heads never cut
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Younger brother of Trần Hiến Tông
reigns.previously: Trần Hiến Tông dies young. His little brother is next in line.
paragraphs: Trần Hạo was about five when his brother died and he became Trần Dụ Tông. For years nothing changed much, because his father, the retired emperor Trần Minh Tông, still ran the court. The boy grew up in the shadow of a man who had already steered three reigns.

Minh Tông died in 1357, and the chronicles say the court fell apart. The young emperor drank, gambled and threw parties while favourites lined their pockets. The old scholar Chu Văn An, tutor to princes, sent up a petition asking for seven corrupt courtiers to be beheaded. Nobody listened, so he resigned and went home to teach. Famine and bandits spread through the countryside.
Dụ Tông died in 1369 without a son. That left a gap at the top of a dynasty that had always kept the throne inside the family.

claims.text: Chu Văn An asked for seven corrupt courtiers to be beheaded, and Dụ Tông ignored him.
claims.note: The Toàn thư records the petition, but its text is lost and the seven are never named.

claims.text: After his father's death Dụ Tông spent his days drinking and gambling.
claims.note: The Toàn thư says so. It was written under the Lê, who liked to show the Trần sliding into decay before the fall.

reigns.hook: Dụ Tông is gone and has no heir. The queen mother picks an adopted grandson, Dương Nhật Lễ, and people start asking who his real father was.

reigns.tagline: The actor's son who sat on the Trần throne for a year
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Adopted son of Dụ Tông's brother
reigns.previously: Trần Dụ Tông dies without a son. The throne needs a new Trần.
paragraphs: Dương Nhật Lễ had grown up as the adopted son of Dụ Tông's elder brother, a Trần prince. The story went that his real father was an actor named Dương Khương, and that the prince had taken his mother into his household while she was already pregnant. The queen mother put him on the throne anyway.

He did not thank her. The chronicles say he turned on the Trần, wanted to take back the surname Dương, and had the queen mother poisoned. That was too much. Late in 1370 the Trần princes, led by Minh Tông's son Trần Phủ, raised troops, took the capital and threw him out. He was demoted and killed. His mother fled south to Champa and begged its king, Chế Bồng Nga, to strike at the Trần.

claims.text: Nhật Lễ was really the son of an actor, not of a Trần prince.
claims.note: So say the chronicles, written by the side that overthrew him and needed him to be a fake.

claims.text: He had the queen mother who made him emperor poisoned.
claims.note: Reported in the Toàn thư. There is no independent account.

claims.text: He planned to change the dynasty's name back to Dương.
claims.note: Another charge from the victors' chronicle; it served to justify killing him.

reigns.hook: Nhật Lễ is dead. His uncle by adoption, the middle-aged prince Trần Phủ, takes the throne, just as the Cham king Chế Bồng Nga sets sail for Thăng Long.

reigns.tagline: Saved the dynasty, then handed it to Hồ Quý Ly
reigns.cameToPower: Led the princes against Nhật Lễ
reigns.previously: Trần princes throw out Dương Nhật Lễ and kill him.
paragraphs: Trần Phủ was a grown man, a son of Minh Tông by a lesser wife, when he led the princes against Dương Nhật Lễ. As Trần Nghệ Tông he got the throne back for the family. A year later the Cham king Chế Bồng Nga sailed up the river and sacked Thăng Long in 1371. The court ran, and the palaces burned.

Nghệ Tông did not want to be emperor for long. In 1372 he handed the throne to his younger brother and became retired emperor, the Trần habit. But he kept real power for the next 22 years, and he trusted one man above all: Hồ Quý Ly, a relative through his mother's family. Nghệ Tông promoted him again and again, and outlived three emperors while Quý Ly's grip tightened. He died in 1394.

claims.text: Chế Bồng Nga sacked Thăng Long in 1371.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư; the Cham attack is also clear from the wider record of his raids.

claims.text: Nghệ Tông's trust in Hồ Quý Ly paved the way for the end of the Trần.
claims.note: The chronicles blame him for it, and modern historians such as Whitmore agree that Quý Ly rose under his protection.

reigns.hook: Nghệ Tông steps aside for his younger brother Trần Duệ Tông, who is set on revenge. Duệ Tông wants to march on Champa himself.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who marched on Champa and never came home
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Younger brother of Trần Nghệ Tông
reigns.previously: Trần Nghệ Tông abdicates and hands the throne to his younger brother.
paragraphs: Trần Kính, now Trần Duệ Tông, was tired of Cham raids. He spent his reign getting ready for one big blow. He drilled troops, built ships and laid in rice, with Hồ Quý Ly in charge of supplies. At the end of 1376 he marched south with a huge army, ignoring advisers who begged him not to lead it himself.

Early in 1377 the army reached Vijaya, the Cham capital. Chế Bồng Nga had set a trap. The Vietnamese pushed forward, were ambushed, and the emperor was killed in the fighting along with many of his men. Chế Bồng Nga then chased the beaten army north and raided Thăng Long again. An emperor killed abroad was a shock the Trần never got over.

claims.text: Duệ Tông was killed in battle at the Cham capital Vijaya in 1377.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư and accepted by all modern histories.

claims.text: Chế Bồng Nga lured the army in with a false offer to surrender.
claims.note: The Toàn thư tells it this way. The story of a trick may soften a plain defeat.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead in Champa. Back home, the old retired emperor Nghệ Tông puts Duệ Tông's teenage son on the throne. Hồ Quý Ly is watching.

reigns.tagline: Tried to stop Hồ Quý Ly and was strangled for it
reigns.cameToPower: Named by his uncle Nghệ Tông
reigns.previously: Emperor Trần Duệ Tông is killed fighting the Cham at Vijaya.
paragraphs: Trần Hiện was about 16 when his father died in Champa. He was emperor in name, but his uncle, the retired emperor Nghệ Tông, decided everything. Chế Bồng Nga kept coming, raiding up the rivers more than once. Through all of it Hồ Quý Ly kept rising, giving orders to armies and filling posts with his people.

By 1388 the young emperor had seen enough. With men he trusted, he talked about cutting Quý Ly down. Quý Ly heard and got to Nghệ Tông first. The old man sided with Quý Ly. He had his own nephew deposed, demoted to a prince and strangled. History calls him only Phế Đế, the deposed emperor.

claims.text: Phế Đế was plotting to remove Hồ Quý Ly when he was deposed.
claims.note: The Toàn thư says so; how far the plan went is unclear, and Quý Ly's version decided his fate.

claims.text: Nghệ Tông ordered his nephew strangled in 1388.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư.

reigns.hook: Nghệ Tông needs a new emperor who won't make trouble. He picks his own youngest son, a boy married to Hồ Quý Ly's daughter.

paragraphs: Trần Ngung was about ten when he became Trần Thuận Tông, and his wife was Hồ Quý Ly's daughter. In 1390 came good news: Chế Bồng Nga was killed in a river battle, and the Cham raids that had terrified the Trần for twenty years ended. But when old Nghệ Tông died in 1394, nobody was left to rein in Quý Ly.

Quý Ly built a stone citadel, Tây Đô, in his home province of Thanh Hóa and in 1397 moved the court there, away from Trần strongholds. In 1398 he made the emperor give up the throne to his baby son and go off to study Taoism. Early the next year Thuận Tông was killed on Quý Ly's orders.

claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư. One account says a Cham deserter pointed out his boat to the Vietnamese gunners.

claims.text: Hồ Quý Ly had the retired emperor killed in 1399.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư, which is hostile to Quý Ly but in no doubt about this.

reigns.hook: Thuận Tông is gone. The new emperor is a toddler, and his grandfather Hồ Quý Ly holds everything.

reigns.tagline: The little boy who gave his crown to his grandfather
reigns.cameToPower: His father was made to abdicate
reigns.reignEnded: Gave up the throne to his grandfather
reigns.previously: Hồ Quý Ly forces Thuận Tông off the throne in favour of his baby son.
paragraphs: Trần Án was about two when he became emperor. His mother was Hồ Quý Ly's daughter, so the last Trần emperor was also Quý Ly's grandson. He is remembered as Thiếu Đế, the young emperor. Quý Ly ran the state from Tây Đô in the boy's name.

Some Trần loyalists tried to fight back. In 1399 the general Trần Khát Chân, who had helped kill Chế Bồng Nga, plotted to kill Quý Ly at a ceremony. The plot failed and hundreds were put to death. In 1400 Quý Ly made his grandson give up the throne to him. The boy was spared because of his mother, and after that he drops out of the records.

claims.text: Trần Khát Chân plotted to kill Hồ Quý Ly in 1399 and was executed with his allies.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư; the chronicle gives a figure of about 370 put to death.

claims.text: Thiếu Đế was spared because he was Hồ Quý Ly's grandson.
claims.note: The Toàn thư says so. What became of him later is not known.

reigns.hook: The Trần are finished. Hồ Quý Ly takes the throne himself, with big plans to remake the country, while the Ming emperor in China watches closely.

reigns.tagline: The reformer who grabbed the throne and lost the country
reigns.previously: Hồ Quý Ly makes his little grandson give up the Trần throne.
paragraphs: Hồ Quý Ly was a man in a hurry. Before he took the crown he had already printed paper money, in 1396, and in 1397 built a stone citadel, Tây Đô, in Thanh Hóa. He capped how much land and how many slaves the great families could hold, and hunted down Trần loyalists. He renamed the country Đại Ngu. In 1401 he passed the throne to his son Hồ Hán Thương but kept the power as retired emperor.

His enemies ran to China. In 1406 the Ming emperor Yongle invaded, claiming to put the rightful Trần back. The Hồ had guns and fortresses, but their reforms had made too many enemies, and the defence fell apart. In 1407 father and son were caught and taken to China. Nobody knows when or how Quý Ly died. Another son, Hồ Nguyên Trừng, ended up making guns for the Ming.

claims.text: Hồ Quý Ly was a cruel usurper who brought ruin on the country.
claims.note: That is the verdict of the Later Lê chroniclers. Modern historians such as John Whitmore see a bold reformer.

claims.text: Hồ Nguyên Trừng became a firearms expert for the Ming.
claims.note: Ming writers credit him with gun-making skills; how much he really changed Ming weapons is debated.

claims.text: Hồ Quý Ly built the stone citadel of Tây Đô in 1397.
claims.note: It still stands and was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011.

reigns.hook: The Ming have Đại Việt and mean to keep it. But a surviving son of Trần Nghệ Tông is about to crown himself Giản Định Đế and fight back.

reigns.tagline: Beat the Ming, then killed his own best generals
reigns.cameToPower: Proclaimed by rebels against the Ming
reigns.previously: Hồ Quý Ly and his son are captured and carried off to China.
paragraphs: The Ming had come claiming to restore the Trần, then annexed the country instead. Late in 1407 Trần Ngỗi, a son of Nghệ Tông who had survived the Hồ purges, proclaimed himself emperor in the south. He is remembered as Giản Định Đế. Two tough generals from the Hồ army, Đặng Tất and Nguyễn Cảnh Chân, joined him.

Together they beat a Ming army at Bô Cô around the turn of 1409, the best Vietnamese victory of the war. Then it fell apart. Listening to slander that the generals meant to betray him, Giản Định had both killed in 1409. Their sons walked out and crowned another Trần prince. Giản Định was soon caught by the Ming, sent to China and killed.

claims.text: The rebels beat a Ming army at Bô Cô around the turn of 1409.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư and accepted by modern histories; the date falls in the last lunar month of 1408.

claims.text: Giản Định had Đặng Tất and Nguyễn Cảnh Chân killed because of slander.
claims.note: The Toàn thư says a courtier poisoned his mind against them; the killing itself is not in doubt.

reigns.hook: Giản Định has thrown away his best generals. Their sons Đặng Dung and Nguyễn Cảnh Dị crown his nephew Trần Quý Khoáng and fight on alone.

reigns.tagline: The last Trần rebel, who chose the sea over a Ming prison
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned by the murdered generals' sons
reigns.previously: Giản Định Đế kills his two best generals. Their sons walk out.
paragraphs: Trần Quý Khoáng, a grandson of Nghệ Tông, was crowned in Nghệ An in 1409 by Đặng Dung and Nguyễn Cảnh Dị, the sons of the murdered generals. As Trùng Quang Đế he fought on against the Ming commander Zhang Fu (Trương Phụ), who pushed the rebels steadily south.

Đặng Dung once broke into Zhang Fu's camp at night and nearly got him, the story goes, but did not know his face and let him slip away. The rebels held out in the hills for four years. At the end of 1413 they were cornered and captured. On the ship to China, Trùng Quang Đế is said to have jumped into the sea. Đặng Dung is remembered for a poem about a hero's work left unfinished.

claims.text: Đặng Dung got into Zhang Fu's camp and nearly captured him.
claims.note: Told in the Toàn thư with heroic colour; the near miss is hard to check.

claims.text: Trùng Quang Đế threw himself into the sea rather than reach China.
claims.note: Vietnamese sources say so. Others say only that he died on the way.

claims.text: Đặng Dung wrote the poem Cảm hoài (Feelings) before his death.
claims.note: It is traditionally his and widely taught, but authorship of such early poems is hard to prove.

reigns.hook: The last Trần emperor is gone. The Ming hold the whole country now, and they mean to make it Chinese.

reigns.reignEnded: Ming army agrees to go home
reigns.previously: Trùng Quang Đế is captured. The Ming hold the whole country.
paragraphs: With Trùng Quang Đế gone, the Ming held all of Đại Việt as their province of Jiaozhi (Giao Chỉ). Zhang Fu's army had done the conquering; the administrator Huang Fu now did the governing. That meant heavy taxes, forced labour in mines and forests, Chinese-style schools and officials, and men taken off to serve in China. Vietnamese books were carted off or burned, later writers said.

In 1418 Lê Lợi, a rich landowner from Lam Sơn in Thanh Hóa, raised a rebellion. The early years were grim. Once, the story goes, his officer Lê Lai put on Lê Lợi's robes and charged the enemy so his leader could escape, dying in his place. The scholar Nguyễn Trãi became Lê Lợi's strategist and wrote his letters to the Ming commanders.

By 1426 the rebels had Ming troops shut up in their forts, and Lê Lợi set up a Trần descendant, Trần Cảo, as a figurehead emperor. The Ming sent a relief army, and at Chi Lăng in 1427 it was ambushed and its commander Liu Sheng (Liễu Thăng) killed. In December 1427 Wang Tong agreed to leave, and early in 1428 his troops marched home. The China deck covers the Ming emperors.

claims.text: The Ming took or burned Vietnamese books to wipe out local learning.
claims.note: Vietnamese sources say so. The scale is hard to check, and many early works were lost in other wars too.

claims.text: Lê Lai died wearing Lê Lợi's robes to save him.
claims.note: Lê Lai was real and honoured by the dynasty, but the story of the swap comes to us with heroic polish.

claims.text: The Ming commander Liu Sheng was killed at Chi Lăng in 1427.
claims.note: Recorded in both Vietnamese and Ming sources.

reigns.hook: The Ming are leaving. Lê Lợi is the hero of the hour, and he is about to make himself emperor and found a dynasty.

reigns.tagline: The rebel king who gave his magic sword back to a turtle
reigns.previously: The Ming army marches home. Lê Lợi has won his ten-year war.
paragraphs: In spring 1428 Lê Lợi took the throne as Lê Thái Tổ, founder of the Later Lê dynasty. Nguyễn Trãi wrote the victory announcement, the Bình Ngô đại cáo (Great Proclamation on the Pacification of the Wu). It declares that Đại Việt has always been its own land with its own ways, and generations of Vietnamese schoolchildren have learned it. Then Lê Lợi made peace with the Ming and sent tribute: emperor at home, king abroad.

Then there is the sword. It came to him in pieces, the story goes: a fisherman netted the blade, and Lê Lợi found the hilt in a tree. After the war, boating on a lake in Thăng Long, he met a golden turtle that asked for the sword back for its divine owner. He handed it over, and the lake became Hoàn Kiếm, the Lake of the Returned Sword.
Power soured him. His old comrade Trần Nguyên Hãn killed himself under suspicion in 1429, and the general Phạm Văn Xảo was executed. Lê Lợi died in 1433, leaving a nine-year-old son on the throne.

claims.text: A golden turtle took Lê Lợi's magic sword back on Hoàn Kiếm Lake.
claims.note: A much-loved folk legend, written down long after his time. The lake's name keeps it alive.

claims.text: Nguyễn Trãi wrote the Bình Ngô đại cáo in 1428.
claims.note: The text survives in his collected works and the Toàn thư.

claims.text: Trần Nguyên Hãn and Phạm Văn Xảo were really plotting against Lê Lợi.
claims.note: The annals record their deaths; many historians suspect a suspicious king clearing out powerful old comrades.

reigns.hook: Lê Lợi is dead, and his nine-year-old son Lê Thái Tông is emperor. The men around him are about to start killing each other, and Nguyễn Trãi will not survive it.

reigns.tagline: The boy emperor who died after a night in the Lychee Garden
reigns.reignEnded: Died suddenly at the Lychee Garden
reigns.previously: Lê Lợi dies after five years, leaving a nine-year-old heir.
paragraphs: Lê Nguyên Long, Lê Lợi's son, was nine when he became Lê Thái Tông. The old war comrades ran things, above all the regent Lê Sát. Once the boy grew up he turned on them. In 1437 Lê Sát was forced to kill himself. Thái Tông ruled for himself after that, and in 1442 held a doctoral exam whose names are carved on the first stele at the Temple of Literature.

That same year he toured the east and called on the great statesman Nguyễn Trãi. Trãi's young concubine Nguyễn Thị Lộ went with the emperor to an estate called Lệ Chi Viên, the Lychee Garden. That night he died suddenly. The court blamed Nguyễn Trãi. He, Thị Lộ and three generations of his family were executed.

claims.text: Nguyễn Trãi was framed for the emperor's death.
claims.note: No real evidence of a plot survives. Many historians think the emperor fell ill and Trãi's enemies pounced. Lê Thánh Tông cleared him in 1464.

claims.text: Thị Lộ was a snake spirit taking revenge on Nguyễn Trãi's family.
claims.note: A folk tale told to explain the disaster. It is not history.

claims.text: Lê Sát was forced to kill himself in 1437.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead before he turns twenty. His heir, Lê Nhân Tông, is a baby, and his mother is about to rule in his name.

reigns.tagline: Crowned in his cradle, murdered in his own palace
reigns.previously: Emperor Lê Thái Tông dies suddenly. Nguyễn Trãi is put to death.
paragraphs: Lê Bang Cơ was a baby when he became Lê Nhân Tông, though he was not his father's eldest son. The eldest, Nghi Dân, had been crown prince until his mother fell out of favour and he was set aside. Nhân Tông's own mother, Nguyễn Thị Anh, ran the government as regent until 1453.

When he took power himself, things were calm. The bureaucracy worked and the borders were quiet. But Nghi Dân never forgot what he had lost. One night in 1459 he and his followers climbed into the palace and killed Nhân Tông and his mother. The emperor was about 18.

claims.text: Nghi Dân had been crown prince until his father passed him over for the baby Nhân Tông.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư; it explains his grudge.

claims.text: The regent Nguyễn Thị Anh had pushed for Nghi Dân's removal to make her own son heir.
claims.note: Later writers say so. The chronicle mainly blames Nghi Dân's mother losing favour.

reigns.hook: Nhân Tông and his mother lie dead. The killer, his half-brother Lê Nghi Dân, sits on the throne, and the officials have to decide whether to accept him.

reigns.tagline: Murdered his way to the throne and lasted eight months
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elder half-brother of Lê Nhân Tông
reigns.cameToPower: Killed the emperor in a night raid
reigns.previously: Lê Nhân Tông and his mother are murdered in a night raid.
paragraphs: Lê Nghi Dân was Thái Tông's eldest son, crown prince as a baby and then dropped. After he killed his half-brother he made himself emperor and tried to win over the court with new offices and rewards. It did not work. To the senior officials he was a murderer who had broken every rule of the family.

Eight months in, in 1460, a group of great officials led by Nguyễn Xí and Đinh Liệt struck. They seized the palace and killed Nghi Dân. He got no temple name, only the title of a disgraced marquis, Lệ Đức Hầu. In his place they crowned Nhân Tông's younger half-brother, the teenage prince Lê Tư Thành.

claims.text: Nghi Dân was overthrown by officials led by Nguyễn Xí and Đinh Liệt.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư.

claims.text: Nghi Dân was a poor ruler as well as a murderer.
claims.note: The chronicle was compiled under the brother who replaced him, so it had every reason to paint him badly.

reigns.hook: The usurper is dead. The officials crown a quiet teenager, and he will become the greatest emperor the Lê ever had.

reigns.tagline: The golden-age emperor who wrote the law and broke Champa
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned by officials after a coup
reigns.previously: Officials kill the usurper Nghi Dân and crown a teenage prince.
paragraphs: Lê Thánh Tông is the Lê dynasty at its peak. He built a Confucian state run by officials chosen in exams, held the exams regularly, and from 1484 had the names of the top graduates carved on stone steles at the Temple of Literature, where many still stand. His law code, the Hồng Đức code, gave women some rights to property and inheritance, unusual for its time. He also cleared Nguyễn Trãi's name.

He was a warrior too. In 1471 he took Vijaya, the Cham capital, captured its king and pushed the border far to the south. Champa never fully recovered. He had maps made of the whole kingdom, finished in 1490. And he wrote poetry, leading a circle of 28 court poets called the Tao Đàn. When he died in 1497, his son Lê Hiến Tông took over a strong, rich kingdom.

claims.text: The Hồng Đức code gave women real property and inheritance rights.
claims.note: The articles exist, but historians debate how far they reflected everyday life and how much was new.

claims.text: The doctors' steles at the Temple of Literature began under Thánh Tông in 1484.
claims.note: 82 steles survive and are on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

claims.text: Thánh Tông captured the Cham capital Vijaya and its king in 1471.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư and in Ming records of Cham complaints.

reigns.hook: The golden age won't last much longer. His son Lê Hiến Tông keeps things steady for a few years, but after him come cruel, greedy and short-lived kings.

reigns.tagline: The steady son who kept the golden age running
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Eldest son of Lê Thánh Tông
reigns.previously: Lê Thánh Tông dies after 37 years, leaving a strong kingdom.
paragraphs: Lê Tranh was in his mid-thirties when his famous father died in 1497, and he took the throne as Lê Hiến Tông. He saw his job as keeping what Lê Thánh Tông had built. He kept the Hồng Đức laws in force, held the palace exams on schedule and leaned on the trained officials his father had promoted.

It was a calm reign, and calm reigns make short stories. Later chroniclers looked back on it as the last good stretch before everything went wrong. Hiến Tông died in 1504, in his early forties. The heir he left was his third son, the sixteen-year-old Lê Thuần.

claims.text: Hiến Tông's seven years were the last stable reign of the Lê for generations.
claims.note: The Toàn thư and modern historians agree that the troubles began after his death in 1504.

claims.text: Palace exams went ahead as normal under Hiến Tông, in 1499 and 1502.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư and in the traditional lists of doctoral graduates.

reigns.hook: The new emperor, Lê Túc Tông, is sixteen and well schooled. The officials are hopeful. They will be choosing again within months.

reigns.tagline: Six months on the throne, then gone
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Third son of Lê Hiến Tông
reigns.previously: Lê Hiến Tông dies in 1504 and leaves the throne to his third son.
paragraphs: Lê Thuần was crowned in 1504 as Lê Túc Tông. He was sixteen, educated in the Confucian classics, and looked like another safe pair of hands. The officials who had served his father and grandfather expected the steady times to roll on.

They never found out. Before the year was over the young emperor fell ill and died, roughly six months into his reign. He had no son. The court had to pick one of his brothers, and the choice they made would become a byword for disaster.

claims.text: Túc Tông died of illness after about six months on the throne.
claims.note: The Toàn thư records his sickness and death late in 1504; no one at the time alleged foul play.

reigns.hook: The court picks his brother Lê Tuấn. His own grandmother thinks it is a terrible mistake, and she is right.

reigns.tagline: The devil king of Thăng Long
reigns.previously: Túc Tông dies after six months, leaving no son.
paragraphs: Lê Tuấn was Hiến Tông's son by a low-ranking palace woman, and his grandmother, the old dowager, thought him unfit to rule. The officials crowned him anyway, as Lê Uy Mục. Once on the throne he had the dowager killed, along with officials who had opposed him. So began the legend of the quỷ vương, the devil king.

The chroniclers pile on the horror: drunken nights, palace women put to death the next morning, his mother's relatives raised high and old ministers living in fear. In 1509 he locked up his cousin Lê Oanh, who got free and fled to Thanh Hóa. There Oanh raised an army and marched on Thăng Long. Uy Mục was caught and made to drink poison in January 1510, aged 21.

claims.text: Uy Mục had his own grandmother killed.
claims.note: The Toàn thư says so, but its account comes from officials who served the line that overthrew him.

claims.text: When drunk, he had palace women put to death.
claims.note: A lurid detail from a hostile chronicle with nothing independent to check it against.

reigns.hook: Lê Oanh takes the throne and promises better. He will soon earn a nickname even ruder than devil.

reigns.tagline: The pig king and his nine-storey palace
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by General Trịnh Duy Sản
reigns.previously: Lê Oanh takes Thăng Long. The devil king drinks poison.
paragraphs: Lê Oanh took the throne as Lê Tương Dực, and the clean start did not last. A visiting Chinese envoy is said to have sized him up and remarked that he was handsome but built like a pig: a pig king (trư vương), heading for ruin. The insult has stuck for five hundred years.

He spent as if there were no tomorrow. He set the builder Vũ Như Tô to work on the Cửu Trùng Đài, a palace nine storeys high, with thousands of conscripted labourers. Taxes rose and revolts broke out. The biggest was led by Trần Cảo, who claimed descent from the old Trần kings and in 1516 threatened the capital.

That same year the general Trịnh Duy Sản turned on his master. Tương Dực had once had him flogged for giving unwelcome advice. Now Duy Sản's soldiers stormed the palace, and the king was cut down as he tried to flee on horseback.

claims.text: A Chinese envoy called Tương Dực a pig king.
claims.note: The Toàn thư quotes the remark, but it is a handy insult for a king the chroniclers despised and can't be checked.

claims.text: Tương Dực built a nine-storey palace, the Cửu Trùng Đài.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư; nothing of it survives. Its builder Vũ Như Tô later became the hero of a famous Vietnamese play.

claims.text: Trịnh Duy Sản turned on the king after being flogged for criticising him.
claims.note: The flogging is in the annals; whether it was the real motive or a tidy explanation is unknowable.

reigns.hook: Trịnh Duy Sản needs an emperor to stand behind, and quickly. Trần Cảo's rebels are almost at the gates of Thăng Long.

reigns.tagline: A boy emperor passed between warlords
reigns.reignEnded: Fled the capital from Mạc Đăng Dung
reigns.previously: Trịnh Duy Sản's men kill the pig king. Rebels close on the capital.
paragraphs: Trịnh Duy Sản crowned a ten-year-old prince, Lê Y, as Lê Chiêu Tông and rode out to fight the rebels. He was killed, and for a while Trần Cảo held Thăng Long itself and called himself emperor. Loyal troops won the city back, but the real winners were the generals, who now carved up the court between them.

Trịnh Tuy and Nguyễn Hoằng Dụ fought battles in the streets of the capital, each ready to crown his own Lê prince when it suited him. Into this mess stepped Mạc Đăng Dung, a tough commander who beat the rival warlords one by one and became the boy's protector. By the early 1520s he held the army, the court and the emperor.

Chiêu Tông, now a young man, saw where this was heading. In 1522 he slipped out of Thăng Long to join Mạc's enemies. Mạc simply crowned the emperor's younger brother instead. The runaway was hunted down and killed on Mạc's orders in 1526.

claims.text: Trần Cảo was a true descendant of the Trần kings.
claims.note: He claimed it to win followers; the Lê chroniclers rejected it and there is no way to test it.

claims.text: Chiêu Tông was killed on Mạc Đăng Dung's orders.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư, which was written by the Lê side, but the fact is not seriously doubted.

reigns.hook: Back in Thăng Long, Mạc Đăng Dung has a replacement ready: the runaway's teenage brother, Lê Xuân.

reigns.tagline: A puppet emperor with the strings in plain view
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Younger brother of Lê Chiêu Tông
reigns.previously: Chiêu Tông flees Thăng Long to escape Mạc Đăng Dung.
paragraphs: Lê Xuân was crowned as Lê Cung Hoàng in 1522 for one reason: Mạc Đăng Dung needed an emperor, and the last one had run away. Nobody pretended the teenager had any power. Mạc ran the army and the government, wore down his brother's supporters, and in 1526 had Chiêu Tông himself put to death.

In 1527 Mạc stopped pretending. An abdication edict was issued in Cung Hoàng's name handing the throne to Mạc Đăng Dung. Soon afterwards the young ex-emperor and his mother, the empress dowager, were forced to kill themselves. After almost a hundred years, the Lê dynasty seemed to be finished.

claims.text: Cung Hoàng and his mother were forced to kill themselves in 1527.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư, written by the Lê side, but not seriously doubted.

claims.text: Mạc took the throne through an abdication edict in Cung Hoàng's name.
claims.note: The Toàn thư reports the edict; the Mạc presented it as a lawful handover, the Lê as theft.

reigns.hook: Mạc Đăng Dung, a fisherman's son, puts on the dragon robe. The Lê loyalists will never forgive him.

reigns.tagline: The fisherman's son who made himself king
reigns.relationToPredecessor: General of the Lê, no royal blood
reigns.cameToPower: Seized the throne from the Lê
reigns.previously: Mạc Đăng Dung makes Cung Hoàng abdicate, then has him killed.
paragraphs: Mạc Đăng Dung came from a fishing family on the coast and got his start, the story goes, by winning a wrestling contest to join the palace guard. He rose through the civil wars to command the army. In mid-1527 he took the throne and had the last Lê emperor, Cung Hoàng, and the emperor's mother killed. The Mạc dynasty had begun.

He didn't stay emperor long, at least on paper. Around 1529 or 1530 he handed the title to his son Mạc Đăng Doanh and, like the Trần before him, kept ruling as retired emperor. Meanwhile Lê loyalists crowned a prince in exile in 1533 and began fighting back from the south.

In 1540 a Ming army gathered on the border to punish the usurper. Mạc Đăng Dung went to meet it, knelt with a rope around his neck, and handed over border districts. The Ming downgraded Đại Việt from a kingdom to a mere commission under him. It worked: there was no invasion. His son Đăng Doanh died in 1540, and Mạc Đăng Dung followed in 1541, still the power behind his grandson's throne.

claims.text: Mạc Đăng Dung began his career by winning a wrestling contest.
claims.note: Told in later accounts. That he rose from humble roots through the army is not in doubt.

claims.text: He submitted to the Ming kneeling with a rope around his neck.
claims.note: Described in Ming records and the Vietnamese annals; the Lê chroniclers made the most of his humiliation.

claims.text: He had the last Lê emperor and his mother killed in 1527.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư, written by the Lê side, but not seriously doubted.

reigns.hook: The Lê are not finished. In 1533 the loyal general Nguyễn Kim finds a Lê prince hiding in Laos and crowns him in exile as Lê Trang Tông.

reigns.tagline: The emperor found hiding in Laos
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned in exile by Nguyễn Kim
reigns.previously: Back in 1533, the Mạc hold Thăng Long and the Lê seem finished.
paragraphs: Lê Ninh, a son of the murdered Chiêu Tông, survived the Mạc takeover by hiding in Laos. There the old Lê general Nguyễn Kim found him, and in 1533 crowned him emperor in exile as Lê Trang Tông. It was a court of a few loyal officers and soldiers, but it gave everyone who hated the Mạc a flag to rally round.

Trang Tông's envoys reached Beijing and told the Ming that a usurper had murdered their lawful vassal. That complaint helped bring a Ming army to the border in 1540 and Mạc Đăng Dung's humiliating submission. Meanwhile Nguyễn Kim pushed into Thanh Hóa, the Lê family's home province, and by the early 1540s the loyalists held the south of the kingdom.
In 1545 Nguyễn Kim was poisoned. His son-in-law Trịnh Kiểm took over the army, and the emperor became his figurehead. Trang Tông died in 1548, aged about 33, leaving a young son.

claims.text: Nguyễn Kim was poisoned by a Mạc defector.
claims.note: The annals say a surrendered Mạc general poisoned him; some suspect his own camp.

claims.text: Lê envoys asked the Ming to punish the Mạc.
claims.note: Ming and Vietnamese records agree that Lê envoys reached Beijing in the late 1530s asking for action against the usurper.

reigns.hook: Meanwhile, in Thăng Long, the Mạc have a new emperor of their own: Mạc Đăng Dung's grandson, Mạc Phúc Hải.

reigns.tagline: The Mạc heir who kept the north
reigns.previously: Trang Tông's loyalists hold the south. Thăng Long stays Mạc.
paragraphs: Mạc Phúc Hải inherited a throne with small print. His father Mạc Đăng Doanh had been emperor in name since about 1530, while grandfather Đăng Dung ran things from retirement. Doanh died in 1540 and Đăng Dung in 1541, leaving Phúc Hải (temple name Mạc Hiến Tông) on his own, ruling a country the Ming now ranked as a mere commission.

He held Thăng Long and the rich Red River delta, the heart of the old kingdom, and the Mạc kept holding civil service exams there. But he lost the south. Nguyễn Kim's Lê loyalists took Thanh Hóa and Nghệ An, and the war between two dynasties settled into a long front line. Phúc Hải died in 1546, and the crown passed to his small son.

claims.text: Under the Mạc, Đại Việt was officially a Ming commission, not a kingdom.
claims.note: From 1541 the Ming ranked the Mạc ruler as commander (đô thống sứ) of an Annam commission; at home the Mạc still called themselves emperors.

claims.text: The Mạc kept holding regular civil service exams.
claims.note: Lists of doctoral graduates show Mạc exams in Thăng Long; the dynasty needed trained officials as much as the Lê did.

reigns.hook: The new Mạc emperor is a little boy. His relatives will fight over him, and the loser will run to China.

reigns.tagline: A child emperor and his warrior uncle
reigns.previously: Mạc Phúc Hải dies in 1546, leaving a small son.
paragraphs: Mạc Phúc Nguyên (temple name Mạc Tuyên Tông) came to the throne as a child, and the grown-ups in his family promptly split. A senior Mạc prince, Mạc Chính Trung, tried to take the crown for himself. He lost, fled north and ended up in China. The winner was the boy's uncle Mạc Kính Điển, who became the dynasty's great general.

For fifteen years the war swung back and forth. Trịnh Kiểm's armies struck north out of Thanh Hóa, and Kính Điển's armies struck south. Commanders on both sides changed sides when it paid, and neither dynasty could finish the other off. Phúc Nguyên died in 1561, still young, and another small child inherited.

claims.text: Mạc Kính Điển was the Mạc dynasty's best general.
claims.note: Even the hostile Lê annals treat him as their most dangerous enemy; he led Mạc armies until his death in 1580.

claims.text: Mạc Chính Trung fled to Ming China after losing his bid for the throne.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư.

reigns.tagline: A figurehead who left no heir
reigns.previously: Back in 1548, Lê Trang Tông dies in the loyalist camp.
paragraphs: Lê Huyên was crowned as Lê Trung Tông at about twelve, and he never got to be more than a figurehead. Trịnh Kiểm commanded the army, ran the government and fought the Mạc, all in the emperor's name. Old loyalists watched uneasily as Nguyễn Kim's son-in-law grew more powerful than Nguyễn Kim's own sons.

Trung Tông died in 1556, about 21, with no son. This was Trịnh Kiểm's moment. The story goes that he quietly asked the old sage Nguyễn Bỉnh Khiêm whether to take the throne. The sage gave the messenger no answer, but remarked in his hearing that if you keep looking after the temple and worshipping the Buddha, you get to eat the offerings. Trịnh Kiểm took the hint and went looking for another Lê.

claims.text: Nguyễn Bỉnh Khiêm talked Trịnh Kiểm out of taking the throne with a riddle about temple offerings.
claims.note: A much-loved story from later tradition; it neatly explains why the Trịnh never became emperors, which makes it suspicious.

claims.text: Trịnh Kiểm had Nguyễn Kim's elder son killed.
claims.note: A long-held suspicion, strongest in sources written under the Nguyễn, who had every reason to blame the Trịnh.

reigns.hook: The search turns up Lê Duy Bang, a distant cousin from the line of Lê Lợi's elder brother. He is about to be emperor whether he likes it or not.
