reigns.tagline: The distant cousin who ran from his own regent
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Descendant of Lê Lợi's elder brother
reigns.previously: Lê Trung Tông dies childless. Trịnh Kiểm hunts for another Lê.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Bang was a distant royal cousin, picked because he had the right ancestry and no power of his own. As Lê Anh Tông he reigned for 17 years and ruled for none of them. Early on, Nguyễn Kim's surviving son Nguyễn Hoàng, wary of Trịnh Kiểm, asked to govern the far southern frontier of Thuận Hóa. He left in 1558, and his family would rule the south for more than two centuries.

Trịnh Kiểm died in 1570, and his sons fought over his place. The elder, Trịnh Cối, went over to the Mạc; the younger, Trịnh Tùng, took control. Anh Tông did not trust Tùng. Late in 1572 he fled south to Nghệ An with his elder sons. Tùng crowned a small son who had been left behind, sent men after the father, and in 1573 Anh Tông was killed.

claims.text: Anh Tông was killed on Trịnh Tùng's orders.
claims.note: The Lê annals, compiled under Trịnh control, tell it carefully; most historians accept that Tùng had him put to death.

claims.text: The sage Nguyễn Bỉnh Khiêm told Nguyễn Hoàng that a strip of the Hoành Sơn mountains could shelter his family for ten thousand generations.
claims.note: A famous saying found in later Nguyễn-era tradition; it looks like a blessing added after the fact.

reigns.hook: Up in Thăng Long, the Mạc emperor Mạc Mậu Hợp is growing up. Trịnh Tùng means to come and get him.

reigns.tagline: The last Mạc emperor of Thăng Long
reigns.previously: Back in 1561, Mạc Phúc Nguyên dies, leaving a baby heir.
paragraphs: Mạc Mậu Hợp became emperor almost before he could walk, with his great-uncle, the veteran general Mạc Kính Điển, running the war. Kính Điển kept the Mạc in the fight for almost twenty years, raiding deep into Thanh Hóa. When he died in 1580 the dynasty lost its best soldier, and the young emperor did not fill the gap. The annals say he was struck by lightning and left half paralysed.

Then Trịnh Tùng came north. Early in 1592 his army broke through and took Thăng Long. Mậu Hợp ran. He was found hiding in a pagoda dressed as a monk and taken to Tùng's camp to be executed. The Mạc were finished as rulers of the delta, though relatives held out in the mountains of Cao Bằng until 1677.

claims.text: Mậu Hợp was struck by lightning and partly paralysed.
claims.note: Recorded in the Toàn thư, written by the winning side; nothing else confirms it.

claims.text: He lost a key general, Bùi Văn Khuê, by trying to take Khuê's wife.
claims.note: The Lê annals give this as the reason Khuê defected to Trịnh Tùng shortly before the fall of Thăng Long; it may be a morality tale.

claims.text: He was caught hiding in a pagoda disguised as a monk.
claims.note: A vivid detail from the victors' annals; that he was captured and executed in 1592 is not in doubt.

reigns.hook: With the Mạc broken, Trịnh Tùng can bring his Lê emperor home to Thăng Long after more than sixty years away.

reigns.tagline: The boy emperor who came home to Thăng Long
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Younger son of Lê Anh Tông
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by Trịnh Tùng
reigns.previously: Back in 1573: Anh Tông is dead, and Trịnh Tùng needs a new emperor.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Đàm was about six when his father fled and Trịnh Tùng crowned him as Lê Thế Tông. He grew up as the banner of the Lê cause in Thanh Hóa while Tùng fought the Mạc. Then came the breakthrough. Tùng took Thăng Long in 1592, and in 1593 he brought the emperor back to the old capital, the first Lê ruler to sit there since the Mạc took it in 1527.

Winning at home was only half the job. The Ming had recognised the Mạc, so the Lê had to win Beijing over too. After years of talks, in 1597 Thế Tông met Ming officials at the border and was accepted, though on terms no grander than the Mạc had got. His envoy Phùng Khắc Khoan went on to Beijing to seal the deal.

Nguyễn Hoàng came north from his southern province to help mop up the Mạc and stayed on at court for years, keeping a close eye on Trịnh Tùng. Thế Tông died in 1599, about 32. By then Tùng had taken the title of prince, and everyone knew who really ruled.

claims.text: The Ming accepted the restored Lê in 1597, but only with the low rank they had given the Mạc.
claims.note: The recognition is well recorded; the exact title and the ceremony at the border are told differently in Ming and Vietnamese sources.

claims.text: Nguyễn Hoàng spent years at the Lê court in the north after 1593.
claims.note: Both Lê and Nguyễn records describe his stay before he slipped back south in 1600.

reigns.hook: Thế Tông's young son takes the throne. Nguyễn Hoàng is still in the north, and he is looking for a way out.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who tried to kill his own minder
reigns.previously: Lê Thế Tông dies, back on the throne in Thăng Long but powerless.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Tân was a boy of about eleven when his father died, and the man who chose him was the lord Trịnh Tùng, conqueror of the Mạc. Tùng ran the army, the taxes and the court. The emperor's job was to sit on the throne, sign what he was given and perform the rites. Tùng also made him family: the young emperor's consort was a Trịnh daughter.

In 1600 a mutiny shook Thăng Long, and in the confusion Nguyễn Hoàng, the governor of the far south, sailed home to Thuận Hóa and never came back. In 1601 he founded the Thiên Mụ pagoda near Huế. He still sent polite words north, but the south now answered to the Nguyễn.
In 1619 Kính Tông, grown up and tired of being a puppet, joined a plot by Trịnh Tùng's own son Trịnh Xuân to kill the old lord. The ambush failed. Xuân was forgiven. The emperor was not.

claims.text: Trịnh Tùng forced Kính Tông to hang himself after the failed plot of 1619.
claims.note: The court annals record it plainly; they were written under Trịnh supervision, so they do not dwell on it.

claims.text: Nguyễn Hoàng used the 1600 mutiny as cover to escape south, leaving a son behind as a hostage.
claims.note: The annals and Nguyễn records agree he left that year, but the hostage detail and his motives are told differently by each side.

reigns.hook: Trịnh Tùng puts the dead emperor's son on the throne. He is about twelve, and a new Trịnh bride is waiting for him.

reigns.tagline: Married to the lord's daughter, marched off to his wars
reigns.reignEnded: Gave up the throne to his son
reigns.previously: Kính Tông plots against Trịnh Tùng and is made to hang himself.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Kỳ came to the throne about twelve years old, the son of the emperor Trịnh Tùng had just driven to suicide. When Tùng died in 1623, his sons fought over the lordship and Trịnh Tráng won. Tráng gave the emperor his daughter, Trịnh Thị Ngọc Trúc, as queen. The Lê and Trịnh were now tied by marriage on both sides, and the Trịnh held every real lever.

In 1627 the Nguyễn in the south refused to pay taxes to Thăng Long, and Trịnh Tráng marched south in the emperor's name to punish them. It was the first of seven campaigns over almost half a century. That same year the French Jesuit Alexandre de Rhodes arrived in the north. He made thousands of converts before he was expelled in 1630. In 1643 Thần Tông stepped down in favour of his son.

claims.text: Ngọc Trúc had been married to a Lê prince before Thần Tông took her as his queen.
claims.note: A well-known story in Vietnamese tradition; the details of the first marriage differ between later accounts.

claims.text: Alexandre de Rhodes baptised over 6,000 people in the north in three years.
claims.note: The figure comes from Rhodes himself, who had every reason to make his mission look a success.

reigns.hook: The retired emperor still lives in the palace. His young son has the throne now, but not for long.

reigns.tagline: Six years on the throne, then an early grave

reigns.previously: Thần Tông hands the throne to his son and retires.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Hựu took the throne at about thirteen while his father lived on in retirement. Outside the palace the world was shaking. In 1644 the Ming dynasty fell in Beijing, and for years Ming loyalists and the Manchu Qing fought over southern China, right up to Vietnam's border.

In the north, Trịnh Tráng was still in charge. In 1648 his army attacked the Nguyễn again and was badly beaten in the south of Bố Chính, near the border. A year later, in 1649, Chân Tông died, still a teenager and with no son. The court had a ready answer. His father was alive, and he went back on the throne.

reigns.tagline: The retired emperor who came back
reigns.previously: Boy emperor Chân Tông dies without a son.
paragraphs: Thần Tông had already reigned for 24 years. Now he was back, a rare second reign. He was still a figurehead. Trịnh Tráng ruled until his death in 1657, then his son Trịnh Tạc took over. The emperor's seal went on Trịnh decisions, and coins went out with his era names on them.

This time the Nguyễn struck first. In 1655 their armies crossed the Gianh River into the Trịnh lands and pushed deep into Nghệ An. For five years the war was fought on northern soil. Trịnh Tạc's son Trịnh Căn finally drove them back, and by 1660 the front was the Gianh again. Thần Tông died in 1662, about 55 years old, leaving young sons behind.

claims.text: The Nguyễn held parts of Nghệ An for about five years, 1655 to 1660.
claims.note: Recorded in both the Lê annals and the Nguyễn chronicles of the war.

claims.text: Thần Tông is one of very few Vietnamese emperors to reign twice.
claims.note: The annals count his two reigns separately, with separate era names.

reigns.hook: The throne goes to his son, a boy of eight. Behind him stands Trịnh Tạc, who has plans of his own.

reigns.tagline: A child emperor while the lord cleans house
reigns.previously: Thần Tông dies after reigning twice.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Vũ was about eight when he was crowned, and Trịnh Tạc did the ruling. Tạc was a stern Confucian. In 1663 he issued a list of moral rules for the villages, and the same edict banned the Christian religion the Jesuits had spread, though Dutch traders were still welcome to sell guns and buy silk.

Tạc also went after the last of the Mạc. They had clung on in the mountains of Cao Bằng since 1592, and in 1667 his army took Cao Bằng. The Mạc leader fled into China, though Qing pressure later let the family back for a few years. The boy emperor saw little of any of it. He died in 1671, about seventeen, and his younger brother took his place.

claims.text: Trịnh Tạc banned Christianity in the north in 1663.
claims.note: Missionary letters report an edict that year; how far it was enforced, and the exact date, vary in the accounts.

claims.text: The Dutch East India Company traded silk for silver and weapons with the Trịnh.
claims.note: Company records in Batavia and the Netherlands document the trade at Phố Hiến and Thăng Long until 1700.

reigns.hook: A ten-year-old takes the throne. Meanwhile Trịnh Tạc is getting ready for one last try at the Nguyễn.

reigns.tagline: The boy who reigned as the long war stopped
reigns.previously: Boy emperor Huyền Tông dies at about seventeen.
paragraphs: Gia Tông was another of Thần Tông's sons, about ten when Trịnh Tạc chose him. His short reign is remembered for one thing, and it was not his doing. In 1672 Trịnh Tạc and his son Trịnh Căn led a huge army south to break the Nguyễn once and for all.

They ran into the great earthen walls the Nguyễn had built near Đồng Hới, and the walls held. After heavy losses the Trịnh pulled back. Neither side had the strength for another round. The Gianh River became a frontier, the north became Đàng Ngoài and the south Đàng Trong, and the two halves would not fight again for about a hundred years. In 1675 the boy emperor died, about fourteen.

claims.text: The 1672 campaign was the last of seven Trịnh–Nguyễn wars.
claims.note: Standard histories count seven campaigns from 1627 to 1672, followed by a long peace.

claims.text: The Nguyễn walls near Đồng Hới were designed by the scholar Đào Duy Từ.
claims.note: Nguyễn records credit him with the defence line in the 1630s; traces of the walls survive.

reigns.hook: Two boy emperors are dead. Next comes a son born after his father died, and he will reign for thirty years.

reigns.tagline: Thirty quiet years while foreigners sketched the court
reigns.reignEnded: Gave up the throne to his son
reigns.previously: Gia Tông dies at about fourteen with the war over.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Hợp was born after his father Thần Tông had already died, and he took the throne at about twelve. Peace held on the Gianh River, so the Trịnh lords Tạc and, from 1682, Căn turned to running the north. In 1677 they drove the Mạc out of Cao Bằng for good, ending a family that had once ruled the whole country.

Foreign traders came and went at Phố Hiến and Thăng Long, which locals called Kẻ Chợ, “the market”. Samuel Baron, a merchant born there to a Dutch father and a Vietnamese mother, wrote a description of the kingdom in 1685 with drawings of its capital and court. In the south the Nguyễn kept expanding, and in 1698 they set up Gia Định, where Saigon now stands. In 1705 Hy Tông handed the throne to his son. He lived until 1716.

claims.text: Samuel Baron's account was written partly to correct an earlier, unreliable book on Tonkin.
claims.note: Baron says so himself: he was answering Jean-Baptiste Tavernier's description, which he thought full of errors.

claims.text: The Mạc were finally driven out of Cao Bằng in 1677.
claims.note: The Lê annals and Chinese records agree on the date.

reigns.hook: His son is a grown man of 26. With a strong new Trịnh lord coming, it will be a busy reign for the officials.

reigns.tagline: A long, calm reign in the shadow of a reforming lord
reigns.cameToPower: His father stepped down for him
reigns.previously: Hy Tông hands the throne to his son after thirty years.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Đường was about 26 when he took the throne, a grown man after a run of boy emperors. It made little difference. In 1709 the lord Trịnh Căn died and his great-grandson Trịnh Cương took over, and Cương was a busy reformer. He rewrote the tax rules, tried to make officials collect taxes honestly and tried to protect village land.

For the emperor it was a quiet life of rites and ceremonies. The Lê still mattered as a symbol: coins, decrees and exam honours all went out under his era names. When Trịnh Cương died in 1729 his son Trịnh Giang took over, and within months the emperor was told to step down in favour of his son. He died two years later.

claims.text: Trịnh Giang forced Dụ Tông to abdicate in 1729.
claims.note: The annals present it as a normal handover; later historians read it as Giang showing who was boss.

claims.text: Trịnh Cương's reforms tried to stop the land of poor villagers sliding into the hands of the rich.
claims.note: His land and tax edicts are recorded in the annals and discussed in modern histories.

reigns.hook: The new lord, Trịnh Giang, is young, vain and suspicious. The new emperor is about to find out how dangerous that is.

reigns.tagline: The emperor history left without a temple name
reigns.cameToPower: His father made to step down
reigns.previously: Trịnh Giang makes Dụ Tông give up the throne.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Phường was about twenty when he took his father's place, in the era the court called Vĩnh Khánh. He was a younger son, put on the throne ahead of his older brother. He lasted three years. Trịnh Giang decided he did not like him.

In 1732 Giang deposed him, claiming he had carried on an affair with a woman of the Trịnh household. The emperor was stripped of his title and made a mere duke, with the insulting title Hôn Đức Công, roughly “the duke of muddled virtue”. In 1735 Giang had him killed. Because he was deposed, he never got a temple name, and history calls him simply by his personal name.

claims.text: Duy Phường was deposed for an affair with a Trịnh concubine.
claims.note: That was Trịnh Giang's charge. Many historians suspect it was an excuse to get rid of an emperor who would not bend.

claims.text: He was killed on Trịnh Giang's orders in 1735.
claims.note: Recorded in the annals, written under the Trịnh.

reigns.hook: Giang turns to the older brother who was passed over. He is in his thirties and knows exactly what happened to the last one.

reigns.tagline: The elder brother who finally got the throne
reigns.previously: Trịnh Giang deposes Duy Phường and calls him a disgrace.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Tường was Dụ Tông's eldest son, passed over for his younger brother. When Trịnh Giang threw the brother out in 1732, Duy Tường was finally crowned, at about thirty-three. He kept his head down. His era was named Long Đức, and he did nothing to bother the lord.

Trịnh Giang was not a steady ruler. He spent heavily on palaces and temples, trusted a eunuch favourite, Hoàng Công Phụ, and squeezed the villages for money. Unrest was growing in the countryside. In 1735, the same year Giang had the deposed Duy Phường killed, Thuần Tông died after only three years on the throne.

claims.text: Trịnh Giang let the eunuch Hoàng Công Phụ run the government for him.
claims.note: The annals blame Phụ for the worst of Giang's rule; he lost his power when Giang was pushed aside in 1740.

reigns.hook: Another brother, a sixteen-year-old, is next. Outside the palace the north is about to explode into revolt.

reigns.tagline: A teenage emperor while the countryside burned
reigns.previously: Thuần Tông dies after three years under Trịnh Giang.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Thận was about sixteen when Trịnh Giang crowned him. Within a few years the north was in uproar. Hungry, overtaxed villagers rose up in the delta, and the Lê princes joined in. In 1738 a group of them, led by Lê Duy Mật, fled the capital to fight the Trịnh from the hills. In 1739 Nguyễn Tuyển and Nguyễn Cừ raised revolts in Hải Dương, east of the capital.

Trịnh Giang hid from it all. He grew so frightened of thunder that he lived in an underground palace. In 1740 the court had enough and replaced him with his younger brother, Trịnh Doanh. Doanh wanted his own emperor too, and made Ý Tông step down in favour of his nephew, Thuần Tông's son. Ý Tông lived quietly until 1759.

claims.text: Trịnh Giang lived in an underground palace because he was terrified of thunder.
claims.note: A famous story in the annals and later writings; it may exaggerate an illness, possibly mental, that made him unfit to rule.

claims.text: Lê Duy Mật led a rebellion against the Trịnh that lasted about thirty years.
claims.note: He fled the capital in 1738 and held out in the hills of Thanh Hóa and Nghệ An until his base fell in 1770.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is a young man of 23. He will sit on the throne for 46 years and live to see the Trịnh lord overthrown.

reigns.tagline: Forty-six years on the throne and never once in charge
reigns.cameToPower: Picked by the lord Trịnh Doanh
reigns.reignEnded: Died weeks after Nguyễn Huệ came
reigns.previously: Trịnh Doanh makes Lê Ý Tông step down.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Diêu became the emperor Hiển Tông in 1740, when the new Trịnh lord, Trịnh Doanh, pushed his uncle Ý Tông off the throne. He went on to reign for 46 years, longer than any other Lê. His secret was wanting nothing. The Trịnh ran the army, the taxes and the jobs from their own palace in Thăng Long. The emperor performed the rites and stayed out of the way.

The north was in a bad way. Hungry peasants rose all over the delta, and a rebel Lê prince, Lê Duy Mật, held out in the western hills for some thirty years. Trịnh Doanh and then his son Trịnh Sâm crushed the risings one by one. In 1775 Trịnh Sâm's army took Phú Xuân from the Nguyễn lords, who were already reeling from a peasant revolt in the south.

Trịnh Sâm died in 1782, and his palace troops, the kiêu binh, rioted to put his elder son Trịnh Khải in charge. After that nobody could control them. In the summer of 1786 Nguyễn Huệ marched up from the south, broke the Trịnh army and handed the government back to the old emperor. Hiển Tông gave him his daughter Ngọc Hân as a bride. A few weeks later, aged about 69, he died.

claims.text: Nguyễn Huệ married the emperor's daughter, Princess Lê Ngọc Hân, in 1786.
claims.note: Recorded in the annals. A famous lament for Huệ, Ai tư vãn, is traditionally credited to her.

claims.text: The kiêu binh, the Trịnh palace troops, made and unmade lords after 1782.
claims.note: The annals and the Hoàng Lê nhất thống chí describe their riots in detail, though both blame them heavily for the Trịnh collapse.

reigns.hook: The old emperor is dead, and his grandson inherits a court full of rival armies. To see where Nguyễn Huệ came from, go back to 1771 and a hill village called Tây Sơn.

reigns.tagline: The tax man who crowned himself emperor
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rebel leader, no kin of the Lê
reigns.reignEnded: Outshone when Huệ took the crown
reigns.previously: Back in 1771, while the Trịnh rule, trouble starts in the south.
paragraphs: Nguyễn Nhạc was the eldest of three brothers from Tây Sơn, a hill village in Bình Định. He traded betel nut and, by the Nguyễn histories, collected taxes until he lost the money. In 1771 he and his brothers Huệ and Lữ raised a revolt against the Nguyễn lords' officials, promising to help the poor. Despite the surname, they were no relation of those lords.

Within two years they held Quy Nhơn. The Trịnh invaded from the north, the Nguyễn lords fell apart, and by 1777 the Tây Sơn had killed nearly the whole ruling family. Only a teenage prince, Nguyễn Ánh, got away. In 1778 Nhạc proclaimed himself emperor with the era name Thái Đức. He made his capital at Đồ Bàn, the old Cham citadel near Quy Nhơn, and rebuilt it.

Nhạc was the politician. Huệ won the battles: he smashed a Siamese army in 1785 and took the north in 1786. Then the brothers fell out, and in 1787 Huệ besieged Nhạc in his own capital. They patched it up and split the country, Nhạc keeping the centre. Once Huệ crowned himself in December 1788, Nhạc's title meant little. He held on to Quy Nhơn until he died in 1793.

claims.text: Nhạc turned rebel after losing the tax money he had collected.
claims.note: The story comes from Nguyễn court histories, hostile to the Tây Sơn, and the versions differ on what happened.

claims.text: During the 1787 siege, Nhạc called from the walls asking how Huệ could cook his own brother's flesh in the same pot.
claims.note: A famous line from later Vietnamese accounts. The siege and the deal that ended it are recorded; the exact words are tradition.

claims.text: Nhạc took the era name Thái Đức in 1778.
claims.note: Coins and documents of the Thái Đức era survive, and the Vietnamese annals record the title.

reigns.hook: Nhạc rules the centre and Huệ the north. In Thăng Long a young Lê emperor sits on the throne Huệ handed back, with no army of his own to keep it.

reigns.tagline: The last Lê emperor, who called in a Qing army
reigns.reignEnded: Fled to China with the Qing
reigns.previously: Nhạc and Huệ carve up the country between them.
paragraphs: Lê Duy Kỳ grew up in the shadow of murder: Trịnh Sâm had thrown his father, the crown prince, into prison and had him killed. In 1786 his grandfather Hiển Tông died a few weeks after Nguyễn Huệ's march north, and the young man was crowned as Chiêu Thống. Huệ soon headed home to the south. He left the new emperor a throne but no army.

Trịnh loyalists came straight back. Chiêu Thống called in the adventurer Nguyễn Hữu Chỉnh to drive them out, and Chỉnh then ran the court himself. Huệ sent an army that killed Chỉnh, and the emperor fled Thăng Long. In 1788 Huệ came north again, executed his own over-mighty general there and left a Lê relative in charge. Chiêu Thống's mother crossed into China to beg the Qing for help.

Late in 1788 the Qianlong Emperor sent Sun Shiyi south with a large army. It took Thăng Long without a real fight, and the Qing named Chiêu Thống king. He spent his few weeks back in power punishing people who had served the Tây Sơn. When Quang Trung's men stormed in over Tết 1789, he fled north with the beaten Qing. He died in Beijing in 1793, aged about 28.

claims.text: Vietnamese memory sums him up with the proverb about carrying a snake home to bite the household chickens.
claims.note: The saying is older than him, but school histories and popular tradition attach it to his appeal to the Qing.

claims.text: Once back in Thăng Long, he took harsh revenge on officials who had served the Tây Sơn.
claims.note: The Hoàng Lê nhất thống chí, by Lê loyalist writers, describes it. Tây Sơn and Nguyễn sources had their own reasons to blacken him.

reigns.hook: A Qing army is camped in Thăng Long for the new year. In Phú Xuân, Nguyễn Huệ is done with titles that mean nothing. He is about to crown himself and march north.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who ruined the Qing army's new year
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Second of the three Tây Sơn brothers
reigns.previously: A Qing army sits in Thăng Long, guarding the puppet Lê emperor.
paragraphs: On 22 December 1788, at Phú Xuân (today's Huế), Nguyễn Huệ declared himself emperor with the era name Quang Trung. Then he went north at astonishing speed, picking up recruits on the way. The Qing commander in Thăng Long, Sun Shiyi, settled in to celebrate Tết, the lunar new year. He did not expect a fight until spring.

Quang Trung struck in the middle of the holiday. His men stormed the Qing forts at Ngọc Hồi and Đống Đa, and on 30 January 1789, the fifth day of Tết, he rode into Thăng Long. Sun Shiyi fled back across the Red River, and many of his men drowned or were cut down trying to follow. Lê Chiêu Thống ran with them and died in exile in Beijing.

Quang Trung then made a smart peace. The Qianlong Emperor recognised him as king, and tribute flowed north again. At home he pushed chữ Nôm, the Vietnamese script, into official use. Then in September 1792 he died suddenly, aged about 39. His heir, Nguyễn Quang Toản, was about nine.

claims.text: Quang Trung sent a lookalike to Qianlong's 80th birthday celebrations in 1790 instead of going himself.
claims.note: Vietnamese tradition and some later accounts say so. Historians still argue whether the envoy was an impostor and whether the Qing knew.

claims.text: The Qing officer Cen Yihan hanged himself as the Đống Đa camp fell.
claims.note: This is the Vietnamese tradition. Other accounts simply have him die in the fighting.

reigns.hook: Quang Trung is dead at about 39. His son Cảnh Thịnh is nine, and in the far south the last Nguyễn prince has waited fifteen years for exactly this.

reigns.tagline: The boy emperor who lost everything his father won
reigns.previously: Quang Trung dies suddenly. His heir is a boy of nine.
paragraphs: Nguyễn Quang Toản was about nine when his father died in 1792. He reigned as Cảnh Thịnh, but his uncle on his mother's side, Bùi Đắc Tuyên, ran the court and turned on the generals who had won Quang Trung's wars. The Tây Sơn began to eat themselves. In 1795 the generals struck back and had Tuyên killed.

In 1793 Nguyễn Ánh attacked Quy Nhơn, and old Nhạc asked his nephew for help. Cảnh Thịnh's army drove Ánh off, then kept the city. Nhạc died that year, and his little realm was swallowed. Ánh came back every dry season, stronger each time. He took Quy Nhơn in 1799, and in 1801, while the Tây Sơn armies were trying to win it back, he sailed north and seized Phú Xuân.

Cảnh Thịnh fled north to Thăng Long and changed his era name to Bảo Hưng, hoping for better luck. It never came. In 1802 Nguyễn Ánh, now calling himself Gia Long, marched north. Cảnh Thịnh was caught on the run, taken to Huế and put to death with members of his family. He was about 19.

claims.text: Cảnh Thịnh was torn apart by elephants.
claims.note: That he was executed is certain. Nguyễn and European accounts describe the method, and the details differ.

claims.text: His uncle Bùi Đắc Tuyên purged the Tây Sơn generals.
claims.note: Nguyễn-era histories tell it this way and were hostile to the Tây Sơn, though the infighting itself is well attested.

reigns.hook: Phú Xuân has fallen and the boy emperor is on the run. The hunted prince from the south is about to take an era name of his own: Gia Long.

reigns.tagline: The hunted prince who united Vietnam and took revenge
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Nephew of the last Nguyễn lord
reigns.previously: Cảnh Thịnh flees north as Nguyễn Ánh takes Huế.
paragraphs: Nguyễn Phúc Ánh was 15 when the Tây Sơn wiped out his family. For years he was hunted, hiding on islands in the Gulf of Siam and living for a time in Bangkok. When his Siamese allies were crushed in 1785, he tried France. The missionary bishop Pigneau de Behaine took Ánh's small son, Prince Cảnh, to Versailles and signed a treaty for him in 1787. France never sent the promised troops.

Pigneau raised money and a few French volunteers himself. Ánh built a base at Gia Định with European-style forts and a modern navy, and he was patient. After Quang Trung's death he ground the Tây Sơn down. He took Phú Xuân in 1801, adopted the era name Gia Long on 1 June 1802 and took Thăng Long that July. For the first time one ruler held everything from China to the Gulf of Siam.

His revenge was savage. The Tây Sơn tombs were dug up and Cảnh Thịnh was executed. In 1804, with Qing approval, the country became Việt Nam. Gia Long built the great citadel at Huế and a law code copied from the Qing. Prince Cảnh had died in 1801, but Gia Long passed over Cảnh's son and chose another son of his own as heir: Prince Đảm.

claims.text: Cảnh Thịnh was torn apart by elephants.
claims.note: That he was executed is certain. Nguyễn and European accounts describe the method, and the details differ.

claims.text: Quang Trung's skull was kept locked up in a Huế prison for decades.
claims.note: A long-repeated story. Nguyễn sources confirm revenge on the Tây Sơn tombs, but the details are hard to check.

claims.text: France never honoured the 1787 Treaty of Versailles.
claims.note: The treaty text survives. The French governor in India refused to carry it out, and no royal army ever came.

reigns.hook: Gia Long dies in 1820. His heir is a stern Confucian who distrusts Europeans, and French missionaries most of all, whatever his father owed them.

reigns.tagline: The iron Confucian who shut the door on the West
reigns.previously: Gia Long dies, leaving a united Việt Nam to his chosen son.
paragraphs: Minh Mạng was the Nguyễn emperor who meant business. His father had leaned on French friends. He wanted a tidy Confucian state run from Huế, and he built one. He redrew the map into provinces under governors he appointed, kept European traders at arm's length, and in 1839 renamed the country Đại Nam, the Great South.

Christianity he saw as a foreign poison. He banned it, and missionaries and Vietnamese Catholics were put to death. In 1833 Lê Văn Khôi seized the Saigon citadel and rebelled, with Catholic support. The siege lasted until 1835. When the citadel fell, a French priest found inside, Joseph Marchand, was executed by slow slicing.

Abroad he pushed west and turned much of Cambodia into a Vietnamese protectorate. In Huế he cast the Nine Dynastic Urns, huge bronze vessels that still stand in the palace. He also raised a famously enormous family. When he died in January 1841, his eldest son took the throne.

claims.text: Minh Mạng fathered 142 children.
claims.note: The Nguyễn family registers list 78 sons and 64 daughters, which is where the number comes from.

claims.text: Joseph Marchand was executed by slow slicing in 1835.
claims.note: Recorded by the Paris Foreign Missions Society. The Catholic Church made him a saint among the Vietnamese Martyrs in 1988.

reigns.hook: Minh Mạng is dead. His son Thiệu Trị inherits a stretched empire, a revolt in Cambodia, and a France whose warships want their missionaries back.

reigns.tagline: The poet king who met the French guns first
reigns.previously: Minh Mạng dies, leaving a tight, closed empire to his eldest son.
paragraphs: Thiệu Trị, born Miên Tông, was a gentler man than his father. He preferred writing poetry to conquering. The Cambodian adventure was costing men and money, and Cambodians and Siamese were fighting back hard, so he pulled his armies out and settled things with Siam. At home he kept his father's ban on Christianity.

The French had not forgotten it. Their warships kept turning up off Đà Nẵng demanding imprisoned missionaries. In April 1847 two French ships opened fire in the harbour and sank several Vietnamese warships within hours. It was a small taste of what Western guns could do, and Thiệu Trị was furious.
He died that November, aged 40. His last big decision was about the succession. He passed over his elder son, Hồng Bảo, and named a younger son, Hồng Nhậm, as heir.

claims.text: French warships sank Vietnamese ships at Đà Nẵng in April 1847.
claims.note: Both French naval reports and the Nguyễn records describe the clash.

claims.text: Hồng Bảo was passed over because he was lazy and loved pleasure.
claims.note: That is the court's own explanation. It was written by the side that won.

reigns.hook: The crown has skipped a son. Hồng Bảo will not take that quietly, and the French ships will be back.

reigns.tagline: The scholar emperor who watched France take the south
reigns.previously: Thiệu Trị dies, passing over his elder son for the younger Hồng Nhậm.
paragraphs: Tự Đức was a scholar on the throne, a poet who loved the classics, and he reigned longer than any other Nguyễn. His elder brother Hồng Bảo plotted against him and died in prison. Smallpox in childhood left the emperor frail, and he never had children of his own.

His bad luck was to rule just as France came for Asia. On 1 September 1858 a French and Spanish fleet attacked Đà Nẵng. Saigon fell in 1859. The Treaty of Saigon in 1862 handed France three southern provinces, and in 1867 the French simply took the other three. That was French Cochinchina.

Then they turned north. Francis Garnier seized the Hanoi citadel in 1873 and was killed by the Black Flags, Chinese irregulars fighting for the court. In May 1883 Henri Rivière died the same way near Hanoi. Tự Đức died that July, leaving three adopted nephews and a court ready to fight over them.

claims.text: Tự Đức wrote his own long epitaph for his tomb, Khiêm Lăng.
claims.note: The stele text at the tomb is his own. He wrote it himself because he had no son to do it.

claims.text: Smallpox made him unable to have children.
claims.note: He did survive smallpox as a child. Blaming it for his childlessness is a common explanation, not a proven one.

claims.text: The labourers building his tomb rose in revolt in 1866.
claims.note: The rising is recorded in Nguyễn sources. Anger at the brutal work on the tomb is the usual explanation for it.

reigns.hook: Tự Đức leaves no son, just three adopted nephews and two powerful regents. The eldest nephew, Dục Đức, is the named heir. He will last three days.

reigns.tagline: Emperor for three days, then starved in a cell
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir in Tự Đức's will
reigns.previously: Tự Đức dies childless, leaving three adopted nephews.
paragraphs: Tự Đức had no sons, so he adopted three nephews. The eldest, Ưng Chân (born Ưng Ái), was named heir. But the dying emperor's will was blunt about him: it criticised his character openly and set regents over him. The two that mattered were Nguyễn Văn Tường and the hard-line general Tôn Thất Thuyết.

Ưng Chân was proclaimed on 20 July 1883 as Dục Đức. Three days later the regents threw him off the throne. Their charge was that he had tampered with Tự Đức's will, trying to keep the harsh lines about himself from being read out. True or not, he had no one at court strong enough to protect him.

He was locked up and given no food, and on 6 October 1883 he died of hunger. His family was left poor and out of favour. But his line was not finished: in 1889 the French put his young son on the throne as the emperor Thành Thái.

claims.text: Dục Đức was starved to death in prison.
claims.note: Nguyễn court records and later histories agree he died in confinement after being denied food.

claims.text: He tried to cut the passage criticising him from Tự Đức's will.
claims.note: This was the regents' own charge, and it suited them perfectly. Historians treat it as at best a convenient pretext.

claims.text: Tự Đức's will openly doubted his heir's fitness to rule.
claims.note: The text of the will survives and is quoted in the Nguyễn records.

reigns.hook: The regents have claimed their first emperor. For the next one they skip the nephews and pick Tự Đức's younger brother, a grown man they think they can steer.

reigns.tagline: He signed France's treaty and paid for it with poison
reigns.previously: The regents depose Dục Đức after three days.
paragraphs: Hồng Dật was one of Thiệu Trị's many sons, a younger half-brother of Tự Đức. He took the throne as Hiệp Hòa on 30 July 1883. The regents expected him to be grateful and do as he was told. Within weeks a French fleet was lying off Thuận An, the forts that guarded the river mouth below Huế.

The bombardment began on 18 August and the forts fell within days. On 25 August Hiệp Hòa's court signed the treaty dictated by the French envoy Jules Harmand. It made central and northern Vietnam a French protectorate, put French officials in the provinces and handed the province of Bình Thuận to French Cochinchina.

Hiệp Hòa now leaned towards the French, hoping they would rid him of his regents. The regents moved first. In late November they forced him to abdicate, and on 29 November 1883 they made him drink poison. He had reigned four months.

claims.text: Hiệp Hòa was plotting with the French to get rid of the regents.
claims.note: The regents said so, and it was their excuse for killing him. The French and court accounts are thin and self-serving.

claims.text: The Thuận An forts fell to a French bombardment in August 1883.
claims.note: French naval reports and Vietnamese records both describe the attack and the quick surrender.

reigns.hook: Two emperors gone in four months. This time the regents want a child, and they choose Tự Đức's youngest adopted son, a frail boy of 14 named Ưng Đăng.

reigns.tagline: The boy emperor who lasted eight months
reigns.previously: The regents force Hiệp Hòa to take poison.
paragraphs: Ưng Đăng was the youngest of Tự Đức's three adopted sons, a nephew by blood. On 2 December 1883 the regents crowned him as Kiến Phúc. He was 14 and in poor health, and everyone knew who really ruled: Nguyễn Văn Tường and Tôn Thất Thuyết.

In the north the French were fighting the Black Flags and Qing troops. In Huế they tightened their grip. On 6 June 1884 the court signed the Patenôtre Treaty, which made the protectorate permanent. To mark the end of the old tie to China, the seal the Qing had given Vietnam's rulers was melted down in front of French witnesses.

On 31 July 1884 Kiến Phúc died, aged 15, after eight months on the throne. Officially it was illness. Rumour said he was poisoned because he had found out about an affair between the regent Tường and Học Phi, the consort of Tự Đức who had raised him. Nothing was ever proved.

claims.text: Kiến Phúc was poisoned to hide an affair between Nguyễn Văn Tường and Học Phi.
claims.note: A rumour at the time and a favourite of later retellings. The official record says illness, and there is no hard evidence.

claims.text: The Qing seal was melted down at the 1884 treaty.
claims.note: French officials watched it done and reported it.

reigns.hook: Kiến Phúc is dead. Tôn Thất Thuyết needs a fourth emperor in a year and picks the boy's brother Ưng Lịch, just 12, who will soon be running for the hills.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who ran to the hills to fight France
reigns.previously: Boy emperor Kiến Phúc dies at 15. The regents need another.
paragraphs: Ưng Lịch was crowned Hàm Nghi the day before his 13th birthday. The real power was Tôn Thất Thuyết, who was quietly stockpiling guns and building a mountain base. On the night of 4 to 5 July 1885 his troops attacked the French garrison at Huế. By morning the attack had failed, and the French were looting the palace.

Thuyết fled into the mountains with the boy. That July a call to arms went out in Hàm Nghi's name: the Cần Vương, or Aid the King, edict. Scholars and villagers across the centre and north rose against the French. In September the French simply crowned someone else, the boy's older brother Đồng Khánh.

Hàm Nghi held out in the hills for three more years. In late 1888 one of his own followers, Trương Quang Ngọc, betrayed him. The French shipped him to Algiers. He never saw Vietnam again. He married a Frenchwoman, became a painter and sculptor, and died in Algiers in 1944.

claims.text: The Cần Vương edict was issued in Hàm Nghi's name in July 1885.
claims.note: The text survives. It was almost certainly drafted by Tôn Thất Thuyết, not the 13-year-old himself.

claims.text: Hàm Nghi was betrayed by one of his own men, Trương Quang Ngọc.
claims.note: French reports of the capture and Vietnamese accounts agree.

reigns.hook: Hàm Nghi is in the hills with a price on his head. In Huế the French crown his older brother, who has a very different idea of how to survive them.

reigns.tagline: The emperor France crowned while his brother fought
reigns.previously: Hàm Nghi flees to the hills and calls the country to arms.
paragraphs: Đồng Khánh was Hàm Nghi's older brother and one of Tự Đức's adopted sons. He had been passed over before. Now the French held Huế and needed an emperor who would work with them, and he agreed. He was crowned in September 1885, while his little brother was still out in the hills calling for war.

He toured the provinces urging the Cần Vương rebels to lay down their arms, and offered pardons. Few listened, and many scholars saw him as a traitor. In 1887 France tied its lands together as French Indochina: Cochinchina a colony, Annam and Tonkin protectorates, with Cambodia too.
Đồng Khánh died in January 1889, aged only 24. His son Bửu Đảo was just three, so the French and the court looked elsewhere for the next emperor.

claims.text: Many Vietnamese saw Đồng Khánh as a French puppet.
claims.note: He owed his throne to the French, and the Cần Vương leaders denounced him as such.

claims.text: His tomb at Huế mixes Vietnamese design with French-made decoration.
claims.note: Finished under his son Khải Định, it pairs lacquer and gilding with imported European glass and tiles.

reigns.hook: Đồng Khánh is dead at 24. The French pass over his little son and reach for a nine-year-old whose father was starved to death by the regents.

reigns.tagline: The modern young emperor France called mad
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the French and court
reigns.previously: Đồng Khánh dies at 24. His son is only three.
paragraphs: Bửu Lân was nine when he was crowned as Thành Thái. His father, Dục Đức, had been starved to death by the regents, and he grew up under close watch. He turned into a curious, restless young man who learned French and loved Western novelties. People said he cut his hair short and drove his own car around Huế.

He also quietly loathed the French, and they knew it. He clashed with the French Résident-Supérieur, the official who really ran Annam. The French began to say he was mad and pointed to stories of violence in his palace. In 1907 they forced him to abdicate and put his son, not yet seven, on the throne.
Thành Thái was held under guard at Vũng Tàu on the coast. In 1916 he was shipped with his son to Réunion, a French island in the Indian Ocean. He was allowed home in 1947 and died in Saigon in 1954.

claims.text: Thành Thái was insane.
claims.note: The French said so. Many historians think it was mostly a pretext for removing an emperor they could not control.

claims.text: He cut his hair short and drove his own car.
claims.note: Told in Vietnamese and French memoirs. The details vary between versions.

reigns.hook: Thành Thái is gone. On the throne sits his son, not yet seven. The French think a small boy will be easy to handle. They are wrong.

reigns.tagline: The teenage emperor who ran away to start a revolt
reigns.previously: The French depose Thành Thái and crown his young son.
paragraphs: Vĩnh San was crowned Duy Tân because the French thought a six-year-old would be easy to manage. He grew up watching them and hating what he saw. As a teenager he began talking to men who wanted the French gone.

In 1916 France was shipping Vietnamese soldiers to the war in Europe. The nationalists Thái Phiên and Trần Cao Vân planned a rising for when those troops turned their guns on their officers, with the young emperor at its head. In early May he slipped out of the palace. But the plot had been betrayed. Within days he was caught, and the two leaders were executed.

He was sent to join his father on Réunion. There he became a keen radio amateur, and in the Second World War he joined the Free French. On 26 December 1945 he was killed in a plane crash in Africa. In 1987 his body was brought home to Huế.

claims.text: The 1916 rising failed because it was betrayed.
claims.note: The French learned of the plan before it began. Vietnamese and French accounts agree.

claims.text: De Gaulle planned to put Duy Tân back on the throne.
claims.note: The rumour followed his death in 1945. It is possible but unproven, and nothing came of it.

reigns.hook: Duy Tân is on a ship to exile. The French want no more surprises, so they pick a prince who has never given them any trouble: Đồng Khánh's son.

reigns.tagline: The glittering emperor who never said no to France
reigns.previously: Duy Tân's rising fails and he is shipped off to Réunion.
paragraphs: Bửu Đảo had waited a long time. Passed over as a toddler in 1889, he was 30 when the French finally crowned him as Khải Định. He gave them no trouble at all. He dressed in glittering uniforms heavy with medals and jewels, and backed the colonial government in public.

In 1922 he became the first Vietnamese emperor to visit France, for the Colonial Exhibition at Marseille. The reformer Phan Châu Trinh, living in France, wrote him an open letter charging him with seven offences against his people. Back home his tomb was rising on a hillside near Huế: grey concrete outside, covered inside in mosaics of broken porcelain and glass.
He had one son, Vĩnh Thụy, and he took him to France in 1922 and left him there to be schooled. In November 1925 Khải Định died, aged 40.

claims.text: Khải Định raised taxes to pay for his tomb.
claims.note: His critics said so at the time and it is widely repeated, but how much of the cost came from new taxes is unclear.

claims.text: Phan Châu Trinh accused him of seven offences in an open letter.
claims.note: The 1922 letter survives and was widely circulated among Vietnamese in France and at home.

reigns.hook: Khải Định is dead. His heir is a 12-year-old schoolboy in France. He will be crowned in Huế, then sent straight back to his books.

reigns.tagline: The last emperor, who handed his sword to the revolution
reigns.previously: Khải Định dies. His only son is at school in France.
paragraphs: Vĩnh Thụy was crowned Bảo Đại in January 1926, aged 12, then went back to school in France. He came home in 1932 promising reform. He made a young official, Ngô Đình Diệm, a minister, but Diệm quit in 1933 when the French blocked every change. In 1934 Bảo Đại married Nguyễn Hữu Thị Lan, a Catholic, who became Empress Nam Phương.

After that he mostly hunted big game and drove fast cars. Then the Second World War reached Indochina. On 9 March 1945 Japan overthrew the French, and Bảo Đại proclaimed an independent Empire of Vietnam, with the scholar Trần Trọng Kim as prime minister. In the north, famine was killing perhaps a million people or more.

In August Japan surrendered, and Hồ Chí Minh's Việt Minh took power in the August Revolution. Bảo Đại announced his abdication on 25 August. On 30 August, at the Noon Gate of Huế, he handed the imperial seal and sword to Việt Minh delegates and became plain citizen Vĩnh Thụy. After 143 years the Nguyễn were finished, and so was Vietnam's monarchy.

claims.text: Bảo Đại said he would rather be a citizen of a free country than king of an enslaved one.
claims.note: The line is in his abdication statement of August 1945. Translations of the exact wording vary.

claims.text: The famine of 1944–45 killed about a million people or more.
claims.note: Estimates range from around 400,000 to 2 million. The Việt Minh's figure of 2 million is the highest.
